title: Nevada flags to fly at half-staff Monday to honor fallen firefighting pilot Christopher V. Andersen - FOX5 Vegas
content: CARSON CITY (FOX5) — Gov. Joe Lombardo has ordered flags at the Nevada State Capitol and all state public buildings and grounds to fly at half-staff Monday, Aug. 17, 2026, in honor of U.S. Forest Service-contracted helitack aerial firefighting pilot Christopher V. Andersen. Andersen died Aug. 7 while supporting aerial firefighting operations on the Widemouth 2 Fire near Three Creeks Reservoir in Fishlake National Forest, Utah. Co-pilot Mike Elliott, 50, also died in the crash of their Sikorsky S-64 Skycrane. MORE ON FOX5: A helicopter battling a Utah wildfire crashes as a blaze kills dozer operator in Oregon Andersen served five years as a helicopter pilot in the U.S. Army, including missions along NATO’s borders during the Cold War. Following his military service, he became a helitack pilot, helping protect communities threatened by wildfires throughout the American West and abroad. He made his home near Lake Tahoe, where he served as a chief pilot and mentor. Lombardo said Andersen earned the respect of fellow aviators for his skill, leadership, and professionalism. “Christopher V. Andersen dedicated more than four decades of his life to aviation and public service, first as a helicopter pilot in the U.S. Army and later flying critical missions and protecting communities across the country and around the world,” Lombardo said. “His courage, service, and dedication to protecting others will not be forgotten by the people of the State of Nevada.” The flag order applies to the Nevada State Capitol and all state public buildings and grounds from sunrise to sunset on Monday, Aug. 17. The order was issued at the request of Andersen’s family. Lombardo signed the proclamation Aug. 14, 2026.

title: Braga v Gil Vicente called off after bout of Bulgarian food-poisoning - OneFootball
content: Get the full live experience with the OneFootball app. This evening’s match between Braga and Gil Vicente has been postponed after a gastrointestinal infection devastated Braga’s squad. The Warriors only have 3 goalkeepers and 7 outfield players available. All other members of the first-team squad have been badly affected by an outbreak of food-poisoning traced back to their trip to Bulgaria for Thursday’s UEFA Conference League qualifier against Dinamo Minsk. The widespread infection was confirmed by a Public Health and Occupational Medicine specialist, who declared the players would be unfit to undertake physical activity for the next 48-72 hours. Braga immediately contacted the Liga Portugal authorities and representatives of Gil Vicente, and thanked the two institutions for their swift agreement to the request to put back the match. The postponement could create early fixture congestion for Braga, given that their Liga encounter against Estrela da Amadora, originally scheduled for next weekend, has also been pushed back (along with Benfica’s fixture against Moreirense), owing to participation in the playoff of UEFA club competitions. Braga will now play Estrela on Thursday 10 September. The club stated that the rearranged date for the Gil Vicente game will be announced shortly. Welcome to the comments! title: The CR-V Is Popular, But This Underrated SUV Is The Better Buy - Top Speed
content: For years, the Honda CR-V has been the safe answer for anyone shopping for a compact SUV. It's practical, reliable, efficient, and one of America's best-selling vehicles for good reason. But popularity doesn't always mean there's nothing better waiting just outside the spotlight. Hidden among the segment's familiar names is an SUV that delivers a more premium interior, a more engaging driving experience, and the kind of refinement that makes every commute feel a little more special. If you're shopping for more than just practicality, it may be time to look beyond the obvious choice. Everywhere you look, you’ll find the Honda CR-V. It is one of the best-selling SUVs in America because it is familiar, proven, and has developed a reputation as one of the most useful family SUVs. Sales volume for the CR-V has exceeded 400,000 over the past couple of years, with 2025 reaching 403,768. These sales reflect the CR-V's trusted reputation and success, but another lower-volume compact SUV could offer a more satisfying driver and owner experience. The CR-V is certainly a top-seller and one of the most popular compact SUVs on the market. It's an easy SUV to shop for because you know what you’re going to get thanks to its reputation, longstanding popularity, and brand recognition. Still, the Honda SUV might not have the driving refinement, engaging experience, or long-term ownership value that you’re looking for in your next vehicle. One SUV brings more driving enjoyment, a refined cabin, and excellent long-term ownership value that could make it a better option than the CR-V for buyers who prioritize the driving experience as much as the ownership benefits. The 2026 Mazda CX-50 takes over where the CX-5 left off, bringing more interior space and a slightly more rugged style to the mix. The Kodo design language comes through clearly in the impressive exterior styling, but the interior is where things get even better. The cabin features high-quality materials, including comfortable seats, soft-touch surfaces, and high-end switchgear. Some trims, including the Meridian Edition, offer a Terracotta leather interior and an outdoorsy feel. A Bose 12-speaker premium audio system is available for some trims, and standard AWD makes it easy to enjoy the control and confidence that Mazda brings to the table. A panoramic sunroof makes the cabin feel airy and light, which is a welcome benefit given the modest rear seat space. The Mazda CX-50 leans heavily into the driving experience with precise steering, impressive suspension tuning, and standard AWD. A turbocharged engine is available, adding power and making it much more enjoyable to drive than most SUVs. The SkyActiv engine tuning delivers maximum torque at lower rpm than most other engines, improving the driving experience. The base engine is a 2.5-liter four-cylinder model that sends 187 horsepower and 185 pound-feet of torque through a six-speed automatic transmission. Turbocharged models have the same engine size but produce 227 horsepower and 310 pound-feet of torque (256 horsepower and 320 pound-feet on premium 93-octane fuel). There’s also a hybrid setup that produces 219 horsepower and delivers increased fuel efficiency of 39 city/37 highway mpg. The Honda CR-V begins with a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, which makes more power than the base CX-50 powertrain, sending 190 horsepower and 179 pound-feet of torque to the wheels. Above that is a hybrid powertrain that generates 204 horsepower. A base Honda CR-V can reach 60 mph in 8.1 seconds, which is slightly quicker than a base CX-50, which takes 8.4 seconds. Going to the turbocharged powertrain, this time is reduced to 6.4 seconds, making it much quicker off the line than the Honda. There’s no denying the Honda CR-V is one of the most popular and highest-rated compact SUVs available. Compared to the Mazda CX-50, the CR-V offers more cargo volume behind the rear seats (39.3 cubic feet vs. 31.4 cubic feet) and more cargo room overall (76.5 cubic feet vs. 56.3 cubic feet). The CR-V is also more efficient, offering 28 city/33 highaway mpg with the base powertrain compared to 24 city/30 highway mpg for the base CX-50. The base version of the CR-V is an FWD vehicle, and drivers can choose that option if desired. The Honda CR-V is easy to recommend, but it is not the right answer for every buyer. If your priorities include a premium-feeling cabin, confident handling, standard all-wheel drive, and an SUV that feels composed and engaging on every drive, the Mazda CX-50 makes a compelling case. Its available turbocharged engine adds effortless passing power, while its upscale materials and quieter interior create an experience that feels closer to an entry-level luxury SUV than a typical compact crossover. Families who need maximum cargo space or the fuel savings of a hybrid will likely be happier with the CR-V, though buyerswho value refinement and driving enjoyment over outright practicality may find the CX-50 to be the more rewarding vehicle to own. But before committing, there's one question most buyers forget to ask: which one will still feel like the right choice after 100,000 miles? Mazda has quietly built one of the strongest reputations for reliability in the mainstream market, and the CX-50 benefits from proven mechanical components rather than an all-new powertrain. Most models use the naturally aspirated 2.5-liter Skyactiv-G engine paired with Mazda's well-established six-speed automatic transmission, both of which have demonstrated strong long-term durability. Just as importantly, Mazda ranked above the industry average in the 2025 J.D. Power U.S. Vehicle Dependability Study, reinforcing the brand's reputation for building vehicles that remain dependable well beyond the warranty period. The Honda CR-V has earned its reputation the old-fashioned way—through years of dependable service and consistently strong owner satisfaction. Whether equipped with the turbocharged or the hybrid system, today's CR-V is built on a mature platform that has proven itself in real-world use. Honda continues to be one of the industry's resale-value leaders. The CR-V's long-term durability is reflected in its consistently high reliability ratings, and Honda also finished above the industry average in the 2025 J.D. Power Vehicle Dependability Study. With routine maintenance, either powertrain is capable of delivering well over 200,000 miles, which helps explain why the CR-V remains one of the safest long-term ownership choices in its class. The 2026 CX-50 has avoided any widespread engine or transmission problems, but buyers should still check that all recall work has been completed. Recent recalls have included an airbag control module software update, a limited trailer hitch mounting issue on certain equipped vehicles, and a front suspension fastener recall affecting a small number of 2025 models. None of these campaigns point to a systemic mechanical reliability concern.​​​​​​​ The current CR-V also has a strong reliability record, though it's not completely free of issues. Earlier 1.5-liter turbo models were known for oil-dilution concerns, while some newer CR-Vs have been subject to recalls involving steering components and fuel-system parts. As with any vehicle, new or used, verifying that recall repairs have been completed is one of the smartest steps before buying. The same buyers who enjoy the Honda CR-V will also enjoy the CX-50, but for different reasons. Drivers looking for a compact SUV that’s much more engaging, fun to drive, and quicker off the line will lean toward the CX-50. Additionally, drivers looking for an SUV with AWD as a standard feature will choose the Mazda over the CR-V. The CX-50 has excellent highway comfort and supportive seating, and turbocharged models can tow up to 3,500 pounds, compared to 1,500 pounds for the CR-V.​​​​​​​ There's a reason the Honda CR-V continues to sit near the top of the compact SUV segment: it excels at the things most buyers value, including practicality, efficiency, and everyday usability. But if your idea of the perfect SUV includes a cabin that feels a step above the competition, standard all-wheel drive, and a driving experience that makes even routine errands more enjoyable, the Mazda CX-50 deserves a closer look. It may never outsell the CR-V, but for buyers who value refinement and character as much as cargo space, this underrated crossover ultimately delivers the more rewarding ownership experience—and that is what makes it the better buy.​​​​​​​ Sources: Honda, Mazda, GoodCarBadCar, Edmunds, J.D. title: Liverpool V Como: Match Review - The Anfield Wrap
content: by Neil Atkinson | Aug 16, 2026 | app, Featured, Featured Writing, Footie, Match Review | 0 comments It’s a long day. A game at 11:30am and a game at 6pm, Jacquet couldn’t have asked for it to have gone any better. He’s bright on the ball and emphatic off it. He senses danger and looks to love defending but he can clearly play. His goal is a lovely back post tap in that a number 9 would be delighted with. He looks like he has been worth waiting for. That, allied with Ronald Araujo’s second-half, means that suddenly centre-back looks the least of Liverpool’s concerns. Araujo is all action; he looks to win any loose ball and that eagerness could prove his undoing. But ultimately he just looks like a real boy and I like that. I like a footballer who looks frisky, who loves the battle, and there will be games where that is a huge bonus. It is a weight off. We’d all start Jacquet against Newcastle but if it has to be Araujo, or a burst of Araujo, then brilliant. It’s funny – Liverpool don’t seem to have signed a bad player for an extended period of time but we have squad concerns. Jeremie Frimpong today reasserts that. He sets up the opener by being direct and confident and playing a marvellous ball and then he defends excellently when the pressure is on for the rest of the first-half. Frimpong is a player about whom there are so many opinions but for me he is just a good attacking right back who actually anticipates danger well. What he can do about the danger from time to time is somewhat up in the air but he isn’t a dope, isn’t a winger, isn’t an oddity. The man who set Jacquet up for that goal was set up by Frimpong for his own. Cody Gakpo has now had two excellent performances in this pre-season. He looks the part, frankly. We’re in a funny position where Liverpool clearly want an exceptional left winger who – in my view – would prove worth the likely fee. But that doesn’t mean strength in depth should have its nose turned up at it. Gakpo is a proven Premier League winner and today he looked like that. At times he didn’t last year. But at times loads of them didn’t last year and indeed, at times we forget they are Premier League winners. Premier League winners in goal, at centre-back, in centre-mid and then a Bundesliga winner up top alongside Alexander Isak. There’s been too much of a desire to forget their class and pedigree. Lots of things don’t look perfect in terms of numbers and in terms of profile. Today there are gaps in the heart of the midfield again at times but when the building is on fire Liverpool at least man the buckets and that helps. Como show the ability to find space and play around corners and a side with more penetration could hurt The Reds. The truth of the situation is nuanced: Liverpool still don’t look quite ready for the start of an arduous campaign. There remains holes at the base of the midfield, especially when Nyoni isn’t on the pitch, which in and of itself begs questions. They look a top attacker down and look cover attackers down. They look off it at set pieces and they don’t progress the ball as well as you’d like through passing. But they look vibrant, ready to pose problems and look like they have goals in the them. Plus there is a key facet here – how does everyone else look? Only Arsenal appear to have most things in hand. Everyone else still has question marks somewhere. And it is these teams that we play starting from next weekend. The thing is, in the short term, we are talking about games. 90 minutes to get the points out of. Last season Liverpool progressively looked like they hated games, the very idea of playing blood and thunder football or coming up against it looked unconscionable to them. It turned their stomach. I’ve been at all the pre-season games (which is weird isn’t it? Should be locked up) and I have seen a Liverpool that wants to play and play. That starts next weekend and I don’t think we are ready. But I think we fancy it. I think we want it and welcome it. I don’t think our opponents are ready either and while they are at home, we know enough to know how that can be used against a side. I’m up for it and into it and I back us to score and I back us to hurt a side. Let’s start there. Two games until the window closes. Five games before the first break. Let’s find a path to eleven points. Won’t be easy. Isn’t impossible. Far from it. I’ve been to all five pre-season games and I have seen enough to be able to delude myself, to perhaps even be genuinely hopeful. You start with delusion. You get to hope. Then you can believe. title: Rangers host Celtic in League Cup quarter-finals - BBC
content: Rangers' reward for knocking out Premier Sports Cup holders St Mirren is a mouth-watering quarter-final against Old Firm rivals Celtic. Derek McInnes earned his first win as boss with a thumping 5-1 victory on Sunday and will now host Celtic. Stenhousemuir, who stunned Motherwell in extra time, will host last season's Scottish Premiership runners up Hearts. Aberdeen will go to Kilmarnock in an all top-flight tie, while Ross County welcome Hibernian to the Highlands. The games will be played across the weekend of 12-13 September. McInnes' first taste of an Old Firm game as Rangers manager was due to be at Celtic Park on Sunday 20 September but will now be across the city. Kilmarnock were the first team into the last eight after beating Ayrshire rivals Ayr United in a five-goal thriller. Aberdeen overcame Dundee 3-0 at Pittodrie on Saturday, Ross County beat Dunfermline 2-1, while Celtic trounced Dundee United 4-0 at Tannadice. title: Springboks predicted team v All Blacks: Rassie Erasmus to curb 'maverick tendencies' - Planet Rugby
content: Springboks rugby players huddle and an inset of Rassie Erasmus. Ahead of the Springboks’ clash against the All Blacks in Johannesburg next weekend, we predict the team that Rassie Erasmus will select for the much-anticipated first Test. South Africa’s head coach is known for rotating his squad, even against the best sides in the world, but we expect them to go in fully-loaded against New Zealand with a team full of experience and quality. Has cemented his position as first choice full-back with a magnificent Nations Championship. Was particularly special in the victory over England by dominating in the air and will surely take the role next weekend. Aphelele Fassi was poor in the narrow triumph against Argentina and made the decision easier for Erasmus. It is not inconceivable that the head coach does something no one expects, given his maverick tendencies, but for the first Test at least he will surely go with the more expected names and that includes Kolbe, who remains one of the best players in the world. Has continued to improve in all facets of the game with the wing a presence in the air despite his shorter stature. Perhaps not as devastating in attack as he used to be but Kriel is one of the best defensive centres in the game and is a real leader in the backline. He has been consistently excellent for the Springboks over the past few years and will be a linchpin if they are to emerge triumphant over the All Blacks in the four-Test series. Has formed one of the best centre partnerships in the world alongside Kriel and it is still going strong. De Allende, despite being 35 in November, remains incredibly dynamic, while he also has an underrated passing game. His individual duel with Jordie Barrett over the next month could be one for the ages. Another scrum-capped wing who is set to take to the field for the Boks. Arendse has a remarkable try-scoring record at Test level and always performs at a high level for the country, so we can’t see Erasmus considering anyone else on that left wing at the moment. Ethan Hooker was promising against Argentina and was stunning in the record victory over the All Blacks last year, but he has been hampered by injury recently. Erasmus has a very tough call at fly-half. Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu is the most gifted of the three and will probably be the favoured option more often than the other two, while Handre Pollard is ultra reliable in the big moments, but Libbok was the playmaker that guided them to two large wins over New Zealand in a 2023 World Cup warm-up and in Wellington last year. With Feinberg-Mngomezulu struggling in the victory over Los Pumas, the Boks may just go with the 29-year-old. Another position where there are plenty of options for South Africa but Reinach has generally been the trusted scrum-half general in the big games. Wasn’t at his best in Argentina but the 36-year-old is still a top quality operator and should get in ahead of Grant Williams. There was a lot of talk about Cameron Hanekom while he was producing an exceptional display in South America last weekend, but that was quickly shut down by Erasmus, who was insistent that Wiese is their first choice number eight. It means that barring injury he will take his place in the run-on side in Johannesburg. Given his importance to the Springboks, they will look to manage his workload ahead of the 2027 Rugby World Cup but, in a series as important as this, Du Toit will start next weekend and likely captain the side with Siya Kolisi probably out of the encounter. Comment: Greatest Rivalry opener to be battle for the ages as Dave Rennie’s resurgent All Blacks and razor sharp duo shine across the park No official update has been given on the hamstring issue Kolisi suffered in Argentina, but it would be a surprise if he has recovered in time for this game. Even if he is fit enough to play, they will likely err on the side of caution in this instance considering his recent injury issues and his age. There would be no point risking him, which means De Villiers is the next in line for that six jersey having enjoyed a fine first few games in Test rugby last month. Has become an important cog in this South African outfit. Nortje has a mammoth work rate and contributes plenty around the field but he is the lineout general in this side and has sorted out some of the issues they had last year. Lood de Jager is an option of course, but he looked off the pace in his return from injury. Like De Jager, the Boks’ record cap holder has not played much recently, but he grew into the game against Argentina and went the full 80 minutes. With that under his belt, he should have enough in the tank to start against the All Blacks. Has been the preferred starter and he should take that role again when Dave Rennie’s men visit Johannesburg. Du Toit isn’t perhaps their strongest scrummager but he is still outstanding in that area, while the tighthead also offers plenty around the field. An easy choice here. South Africa don’t necessarily lack depth at hooker with Jan-Hendrik Wessels and Johan Grobbelaar outstanding front-rowers, but it is difficult to see anyone other than Marx starting the first three Tests at the very least. One of the best players of his generation. Has gone from a key member of the Bomb Squad to guaranteed starter. Sets the tone in the set-piece while also being a destructive carrier with ball in hand. Can get his side on the front foot in several ways and is undoubtedly the premier loosehead in the sport at the moment. Bench: 16 Jan-Hendrik Wessels, 17 Gerhard Steenekamp, 18 Zachary Porthen, 19 Cobus Wiese, 20 Cameron Hanekom, 21 Andre Esterhuizen, 22 Grant Williams, 23 Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu There are a few tight battles for the bench and beginning at hooker it will likely be between Wessels and Grobbelaar, but we reckon Erasmus will go for the former. Steenekamp is an obvious call at loosehead as he is another outstanding scrummager but tighthead is much tougher for the Boks coaches. Wilco Louw is the best in the set-piece but youngster Zachary Porthen has been improving every game in that area and offers more around the field. Nick Mallett has a theory that Louw’s influence has been reduced due to World Rugby depowering the scrum and, with Porthen a standout in Argentina, the 22-year-old could sneak it. The replacement lock is also difficult but Cobus Wiese was impactful against Los Pumas and, quite frankly, is in better shape than De Jager at the moment. Franco Mostert is also in the wider training squad but he has not played since June. As for the replacement loose forward(s), they do not lack for options but Hanekom’s performance against Los Pumas could be rewarded while hybrid player Andre Esterhuizen, providing he has recovered from his head injury, effectively allows South Africa to have both a 6-2 and 5-3 bench. That leaves the out-and-out backline spots where we predict Williams to fill one and Feinberg-Mngomezulu the other. The latter was not exactly stellar against Argentina but he is a special talent and, perhaps most importantly, can play at fly-half, centre and full-back. title: Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing: The Last Supercharged V8 Super Sedan America Will Probably Ever Build - Top Speed
content: The super sedan as we've known it, naturally aspirated or supercharged, rear-wheel-drive, unapologetically analog, is running out of road. Regulatory pressure, electrification mandates, and shrinking sedan demand have pushed nearly every rival toward hybrid assistance or turbocharged downsizing. Yet one holdout remains. A car that pairs a supercharged V8 with an honest-to-goodness manual gearbox and no electric motor in sight. It undercuts pricier German competition by tens of thousands of dollars and, unusually for a six-figure performance sedan, is holding its value rather than shedding it. This is the story of the last car of its kind, and why waiting to buy one is starting to look like the riskier move. For decades, the super sedan formula was simple: take a mainstream four-door, stuff in a big engine, stiffen everything, and sell it to buyers who wanted supercar performance with room for car seats. BMW's M5, Mercedes-AMG's E63, and Audi's RS7 built entire identities around this idea, each one-upping the others with more cylinders, more boost, more horsepower. That formula is unraveling faster than most enthusiasts expected. The latest BMW M5 now carries a plug-in hybrid powertrain, adding over 1,000 pounds of mass in exchange for hybrid-assisted power. Mercedes-AMG has similarly shifted the E63 toward electrification, with the C63 already having swapped its V8 for a turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid setup. Audi's RS7 remains V8-powered for now, but industry signals point toward the same electrified direction as emissions regulations tighten globally. The shift isn't really about performance; these hybrid systems often produce blistering power figures. It's about character. A 5,400-pound sedan with a battery pack and electric motors drives differently than one built purely around a mechanical relationship between throttle, supercharger, and rear wheels. Purists argue that something is lost in translation, even when the spec sheet says otherwise. Against that backdrop, one nameplate has become an accidental holdout. A car built before this transition fully took hold, powered by a genuinely enormous supercharged V8, still offered with a manual transmission, and still purely internal combustion. Nobody planned for it to become the last of its kind this quickly. But with its window of production narrowing and no direct successor confirmed to carry the same formula forward, it's increasingly looking like America's final unfiltered super sedan—or at least the last one we're likely to see for a very long time. That car is the 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, and it makes its case with numbers that sound almost anachronistic in 2026. Under the hood sits a 6.2-liter supercharged V8 producing 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet of torque, figures that would have topped the segment outright a decade ago and still comfortably compete with anything German rivals can muster today. What makes the Blackwing genuinely unusual isn't just the output, but how buyers can access it. Cadillac still offers a six-speed manual transmission alongside a 10-speed automatic, a combination that has all but vanished from this segment. Reviewers have noted that the manual isn't a token gesture either; it's a properly weighted, mechanically satisfying gearbox that rewards drivers willing to work for their acceleration. Speaking of acceleration, the automatic-equipped CT5-V Blackwing has been recorded hitting 0-60 mph in roughly 3.4 seconds, with the manual only slightly behind at 3.6 seconds. Those numbers put it in the same performance bracket as cars costing significantly more, and they arrive without sacrificing everyday usability. Reviewers consistently point to the Blackwing's Tour driving mode and magnetic ride control as proof that Cadillac tuned this car to be genuinely livable and not just track-focused. It's the kind of chassis calibration that lets an owner drive to work in comfort and then find a back road on the weekend without the car fighting them the entire way. The result is a sedan that reads as a full-throated final statement rather than a compromise. Cadillac built the Blackwing without hedging on displacement, without adding electrification, and without diluting the manual option, even as competitors moved in the opposite direction. Performance numbers only tell half the story; pricing is where the Blackwing's case becomes genuinely compelling. For 2026, the CT5-V Blackwing carries a base MSRP of $98,900 before destination and gas guzzler fees, a figure that positions it well below the segment's German benchmarks. The current BMW M5, now saddled with plug-in hybrid hardware, starts north of $123,000, putting roughly $24,000 of daylight between it and the Cadillac. The gap widens further against the Audi RS7, which starts closer to $132,700, nearly $34,000 more than the Blackwing's asking price. Even accounting for standard equipment differences, that's not a marginal discount; it's the kind of price separation that changes which shoppers cross-shop these cars at all. What makes this pricing dynamic particularly notable is that the Blackwing isn't winning on a technicality. It isn't undercutting rivals by offering less power or a smaller engine; if anything, its supercharged V8 delivers output competitive with, or exceeding, hybrid-assisted alternatives that cost tens of thousands more. Buyers aren't being asked to accept a lesser car for less money; they're getting comparable or superior straight-line performance, a manual gearbox unavailable elsewhere in the segment, and a lower sticker price simultaneously. Most performance sedans at this price point depreciate aggressively within three years. The Blackwing is doing something almost no one expected — and the used market numbers tell a story that changes the math for anyone still on the fence.​​​​​​​ Six-figure performance sedans typically depreciate hard. Complex hybrid systems, expensive maintenance, and shifting buyer tastes usually combine to punish resale values within a few years of purchase. The CT5-V Blackwing is defying that pattern in a way that's caught the attention of the used market. Average used sale prices for the Blackwing hover around $91,457—remarkably close to its original MSRP—and clean, low-mileage examples have sold for as much as $111,000, above what many paid new. Perhaps most striking, early 2022 model-year Blackwings have reportedly lost only around 10 percent of their value over four years, a depreciation curve that would be unusual for almost any performance sedan, let alone one wearing a Cadillac badge in a segment historically dominated by German prestige. That said, the resale story isn't universally rosy, and it's worth being upfront about the exception. The limited-run 120th Anniversary Edition, which carried a considerably higher MSRP of $142,530, has been reported losing nearly $50,000 in value after just a few thousand miles. That's a meaningful counterpoint, and it suggests the Blackwing's depreciation resistance applies most reliably to base and moderately optioned cars rather than heavily marked-up special editions where buyers paid a significant premium at the outset. Scoped correctly, though, the pattern holds: a well-optioned but not excessively loaded Blackwing appears to be one of the rare modern performance sedans that behaves more like a collectible than a depreciating asset, exactly the kind of signal that tends to precede genuine collector-market attention. If there was any doubt that the collector market has already started forming around this car, Cadillac's own product decisions confirm it. For 2026, the brand introduced an F1 Collector Series variant limited to just 26 units, bumping the supercharged V8's output to 685 horsepower. A production run that small isn't a mainstream sales strategy; it's a deliberate move to create scarcity around a car that's already becoming a send-off. That's the broader signal worth paying attention to. Cadillac isn't positioning the Blackwing as an ongoing, iterative nameplate with a clear multi-generation future in this exact form. Every cue—the shrinking field of direct rivals, the industry-wide pivot toward electrification, the low-volume special editions—points toward a car nearing the end of its production life in its current, unhybridized form. For prospective buyers, that context changes the calculus considerably. Waiting for a discount, or assuming another manual, V8-powered, non-hybrid super sedan will simply appear from a rival automaker, looks increasingly like wishful thinking. The used market data already suggests other buyers have reached the same conclusion, which is part of why prices have stayed firm rather than sliding the way they typically would for a car this powerful and this expensive. The Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing isn't just a strong performance sedan competing on specs and price. It's a closing chapter, quite possibly the last of its kind that American buyers will get to choose with a stick shift and no battery pack in sight. For anyone who's been circling one, the market is already signaling that the window to buy in before values climb further is narrower than it looks. We want to hear from you. title: How Much It Costs To Replace A Honda CR-V Hybrid Battery In 2026 - Top Speed
content: Nikesh Kooverjee has been contributing to the automotive sphere for 11 years. His previous roles include Digital Editor at CAR South Africa and associate editor at CarBuzz. He has always had a strong affinity for cars from a young age, having grown up in a family of classic Mercedes-Benz collectors. He has perused through numerous automotive literature in a bid to further his knowledge and understanding of all things car-related. He eventually went to attain a degree in Media and Writing, English Literature, and Film and Television Studies at the University of Cape Town while working as a go-kart marshal in-between hours. His passions remain automotive, with an increased interest in electromobility and autonomous technologies. The current-generation Honda CR-V Hybrid has been enjoying immense success in the U.S. new vehicle market for several valid and convincing reasons. The Honda CR-V has been the     Japanese brand's most popular model line for quite some time, thanks to its dependable and versatile characteristics. With time and usage, the Honda CR-V Hybrid will need its battery pack replaced. Thankfully, this occurs very late in its life cycle, but it is a fairly considerable and relatively financially heavy repair that you have to conduct. Honda is transparent about parts pricing, giving us a clear idea of how much a replacement will cost you today. The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid employs a front-wheel drive and optional all-wheel drive system that increases the compact SUV's appeal in the competitive market. It represents a natural evolution of the brand's electrification strategy, which pursues multiple power sources. This includes full electrification and hydrogen fuel-cell technology, but it's clear that gasoline-electric hybrid remains its primary focus at this time. Just bear in mind that these prices will be vastly different when the time comes to have a new one fitted after about two decades. Like many other brands, Honda anticipates that replacing the battery pack on its hybrids will be relatively more affordable in the future, even when taking inflation into account. Honda's online parts catalog for the CR-V Hybrid indicates that a new HEV battery pack module costs $3,515 before taxes and discounts, but this includes all auxiliary components that you wouldn't typically need unless your housing sustains damage due to a collision or manufacturer fault. Select Honda dealership websites indicate that you can expect to pay around $2,000 for a new hybrid battery in the best-case scenario, which we think is a bit of a conservative figure. CR-V owner forum users have indicated that older Honda CR-V Hybrid battery replacements typically cost around $1,900 for parts, excluding labor via an independent workshop, which sounds reasonably accurate. Parts are likely to take up the bulk of the cost, with battery replacement labor estimated to be around $500 and $800 depending on whether you take your vehicle to a Honda-accredited service center or an independent workshop. Replacing the battery pack on an HEV is a much easier task than a    battery module replacement for an EV, but it does require some level of stripping, as the large pack is typically located beneath the rear bench. Honda includes its standard three-year or 36,000-mile limited warranty and five-year or 60,000-mile powertrain warranty with every CR-V Hybrid sale. You also get a five-year corrosion warranty over an unlimited mile range. If you have a replacement part fitted, the manufacturer covers this for one year. Accessories get a three-year or 36,000-mile warranty. All hybrid systems are covered for three years or 36,000 miles, but the battery pack gets the     market-standard eight years and 100,000-mile coverage. For peace of mind while on the road, you also get a 36-month or 36,000-mile roadside warranty in the package. There are also in-house extended warranty packages that vary in years and miles if you intend to keep the car for longer. The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid benefits from     good overall mechanical reliability, predominately thanks to the dependable nature of its L-Series ICE unit, but the direct-drive system also omits a lot of possible mechanical faults. J.D. Power gives the entire range an 83/100 consumer-verified overall score, consisting of 83/100 for quality and reliability, 79/100 for the driving experience, 86/100 for resale, and 83/100 for dealership experience. According to iSeeCars, the CR-V has an average lifespan of around 169,626 miles or about 13.9 years, with a 30.4 percent chance of reaching 200,000 miles. The publication grants it a 7.9/10 for reliability, placing it in second place for both most reliable crossover SUV and most reliable small SUV categories. CarEdge placed the CR-V's five-year cost at $36,935, which is just over $1,000 more than the RAV4. In terms of maintenance costs, CarEdge puts the dollar amount at $7,636 over the first ten years of ownership, with a 21.74 percent chance it will require major repairs - both of those figures are lower than the average for similar SUVs. Honda only offers one gasoline-electric hybrid configuration for the CR-V, which is an Atkinson-cycle 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with a pair of permanent-magnet motors. The     Honda CR-V is the brand's most popular model in its monthly sales charts, and features this drivetrain with 204 horsepower and 274 pound-feet of torque state-of-tune. You can have this as a front-wheel drive or all-wheel drive model, the latter of which incorporates a conventional driveline to the rear axle rather than an additional electric motor. The brand's hybrids don't feature a conventional transmission, but rather a     direct-drive eCVT unit similar to what you would find in an EV. The front-wheel drive CR-V benefits from an appealing 43/36/40 MPG EPA consumption estimate on the city/highway/combined cycle. The all-wheel drive model returns a slightly worse 40/34/37 MPG result. The 14-gallon gasoline tank gets you 560 miles of range in front-wheel drive guise, which the all-wheel drive system lowers to 518 miles. Honda's hybrid system is a series-parallel variation, which means it allows the operation of the electric motor independently. The front-wheel drive model is likely to save you $3,250 in fuel costs over five years, compared to the average new vehicle currently being sold in the U.S. This will cost an estimated $1,550 to refuel over a year and $2.56 to drive 25 miles. A full tank of gas will cost around $57. Beyond the battery pack, the 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid benefits from     competitively low five-year ownership costs, according to Edmunds. The publication highlights that you can expect to spend $5,638 on maintenance, $601 on repairs, and $11,399 on depreciation. You'll also likely spend around $6,272 on fuel. CarEdge indicates that the model will cost you $39,524 to own over five years and 60,000 miles, which accounts for $13,059 on depreciation, $7,700 on fuel, and $2,440 on maintenance. Furthermore, iSeeCars issues the CR-V Hybrid range with a $13,792 or 38.7-percent depreciation rate after five years, which is a bit worse than its main rivals. According to Honda's own estimations, you can expect the CR-V Hybrid battery packs to last six to 10 years or up to 100,000 miles. Other Honda hybrid battery options can last for     10 years or even closer to 150,000 miles, but this is entirely dependent on your care practices and usage. Several factors contribute to wear on a Honda hybrid battery. Key among them is high heat, which accelerates degradation in the lithium-ion cells commonly used in Honda’s hybrid models. Frequent high-power discharge and recharge cycles also add strain, especially in stop-and-go traffic, where the hybrid system toggles between engine and battery power more often. Deep discharges, or letting the battery drain close to empty before recharging, wear down cells faster than shallow cycles, but the vehicle's software usually mitigates this from happening. The     2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid relies on the Honda Maintenance Minder system to calculate service intervals based on real-time engine conditions. Technicians perform routine oil changes, tire rotations, and multi-point inspections every 7,500 to 10,000 miles. Cabin air filters and engine air filters require replacement every 15,000 to 30,000 miles. Midlife servicing at 45,000 to 60,000 miles requires transmission fluid renewals, brake fluid flushes, and rear differential fluid changes on all-wheel-drive models. Long-term maintenance milestones reaching 90,000 to 120,000 miles demand spark plug replacements, engine coolant flushes, and mechanical valve inspections. Basic upkeep costs remain moderate throughout early ownership, averaging between $400 and $600 per year for standard maintenance. Major mileage intervals requiring transmission fluids, spark plugs, and brake flushes push individual service visits toward $800 or more depending on dealer labor rates. The factory warranty covers the high-voltage hybrid traction battery for eight years or 100,000 miles under standard federal regulations, which minimizes early out-of-pocket hybrid expenses. California emissions states extend this high-voltage component coverage to 10 years or 150,000 miles. Sixth-generation Honda CR-V models spanning 2023 through 2026 face several safety recalls. A major steering gearbox recall targets an improperly manufactured worm wheel that swells under ambient heat and humidity. This defect causes a sticky steering feel, and dealers resolve the condition by replacing the worm gear spring and adding fresh lubricant. Separate fuel system recalls address high-pressure fuel pumps and loose fuel hose connections that crack, leak, or cause engine stalls. Additional safety recalls involve passenger seat weight sensors that short-circuit from humidity and     cause improper airbag deployment. Source: Honda, EPA, J.D. title: Bulls v All Blacks: Winners and losers as Test hopefuls 'solidify' positions while Bulls' 'best player' sends 'reminder' to Rassie Erasmus - Planet Rugby
content: Leroy Carter (left) and Dave Rennie (inset) are among the key winners from the All Blacks' win over the Bulls Following the All Blacks’ 50-19 win over the Bulls at Loftus Versfeld, here is our take on the key winners and losers from the third game of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series. After arguably one of the standout performances for his side in their win over the Stormers, Leroy Carter was back in the thick of the action on Saturdya against the Bulls. His evening started with a superb injection of quality to create Josh Moorby’s try, coming off his wing and almost becoming an extra 13, which only set the tone for the rest of his work. In total, he ended the night with a game-high 16 carries alongside 68 metres, all while bagging a hat-trick. This performance in isolation would certainly be enough to push his case for Test selection, especially considering the injury to Caleb Clarke, but with it also coming off the back of a big game in Cape Town, it only solidifies that feeling further. It’s not been smooth sailing for the All Blacks scrum thus far this series, especially against the Stormers, but this was a very complete scrummaging effort from Dave Rennie’s pack. The starting front-row of Xavier Numia, Codie Taylor and Tyrel Lomax just seemed to have the Bulls’ number at every turn, winning a few penalties for their efforts, and that dominance was later matched by the combination of Samisoni Taukei’aho, George Bower and Siale Lauaki in the latter stages too. What’s even more pleasing from Rennie’s point of view is that there’s real improvement in this area. The attacking intent was there from the run-on front-row, with Lomax arguably leading the hunt while Numia’s powerful follow-through got good change as well, and the replacements also came into their own after a tough time of it in Cape Town. Bulls player ratings: Captain fantastic displays ‘one-man masterclass’ while little too late bench ‘save face’ If you’re playing against the Springboks, you need your scrum to really stand up, and while it will certainly be another step up next weekend, this was a notable statement from the All Blacks in this department. He certainly put his hand up for a Test jersey come Saturday, when the Springboks welcome New Zealand to Ellis Park. The German-born loose forward made two technically brilliant turnovers just when the All Blacks looked to be against the cosh, in what was an aggressive and very deliberate performance. He made 10 carries just in the second half and finished with a team high of 13 tackles. There’s certainly no reason for Rennie not to include him in the Test 23 after that performance. The double World Rugby Player of the Year has not seemed worthy of that title for quite some time, certainly not in an All Black shirt. But with concern surrounding Damian McKenzie’s fitness, and Richie Mo’unga returning to the squad, a less pressurising spot at full-back could well be exactly what Barrett needs to rediscover his form. Well, against the Bulls he certainly seemed to be heading back to his absolute best, injecting himself into the attack wonderfully, assisting Moorby’s first try with a perfectly timed pass, before playing a pivotal role in the winger’s second score. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. He appeared to be relaxed in his playing style, while the number 10 position was occupied and the responsibility absorbed. Time will tell what the future holds, but Barrett at 15 does not seem like a bad idea after that performance. The entire team played their socks off in a game that could so easily have been treated as a dead rubber. Your inexperienced youth are becoming fully fledged members of the team. Momentum is building within the squad as they head into what promises to be the most challenging and important four-Test series of your career, and faith is growing within the loyal but expectant fanbase back home. What goes up must indeed come down, but right now, Rennie is flying high. He’s yet to lose a game in charge of the All Blacks, and with a stacked team to choose from heading into next weekend’s Test, he’ll certainly fancy his chances. The Bulls’ best player by a country mile. Right from the initial stages of the game, he was the key driver for the Bulls, and didn’t relax until the final whistle. Each contact he made was brutal, and every time was without hesitation, racking up over 60 metres with the ball in hand to give his side some very rare, but needed, front-foot ball. All Blacks player ratings: Wingers make Dave Rennie’s selection job ‘incredibly difficult’ for Springboks Test while Beauden Barrett hits back Now 35-years-old, he’s not played for the Springboks in five years, but a performance like that, on such a stage, may send a little reminder to Rassie Erasmus that he’s not quite done yet. With the Springboks sending Elrigh Louw and Johan Grobbelaar to the Bulls for this fixture, in an effort to get them some game time ahead of the Test series, that saw Mpilo Gumede and Jaundre Schoeman drop out of the squad. While this was a major boost for the Bulls ahead of the game, it would have really stung for the axed duo to be taken out of the squad and denied a rare chance to take on the All Blacks. Things like that have been a major positive to emerge from this tour to date, so it is a real shame for the pair. Injuries have become a bit of a theme for the All Blacks this tour, and tonight they suffered two further concerns that will leave Rennie sweating. Scrum-half Cortez Ratima, who has featured in all three tour games to date, came off with a knock to his knee, while Numia also reported back with a tight Achilles. However, while these will cause somewhat of a concern amid the backdrop of Cam Roigard’s calf issue and Caleb Clarke, Billy Proctor and George Bell being sent home with injuries, it was more of a precaution to take them off. title: Arsenal v Man City: Community Shield 2026 - does winning trophy lead to good season? - BBC
content: Dean Henderson's penalty shootout heroics helped Crystal Palace win the 2025 Community Shield The Community Shield takes place between two teams who will be hoping to battle it out for the Premier League this season. English champions Arsenal take on runners-up and FA Cup winners Manchester City at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Sunday. But do the stats suggest winning the curtain-raiser in the Welsh capital would indicate a successful season ahead? And what of the goalscorers? Considering the current Premier League champions play in the game every season it is surprisingly rare for the Community Shield winners to go on to win the league. Since the Premier League started in 1992-93, only eight of the 34 winners of the Charity or Community Shield have done so. Five of those happened in a six-year spell from 2005 until 2010. Manchester City, in 2019, were the last team to do so - and before that it was Alex Ferguson's Manchester United in 2011. Only one of the past 15 winners of the Community Shield have gone on to become champions that season. Since 1992 the teams who lose the Community Shield have won more league titles that season - 10 in total, including Manchester City for three years in a row between 2021 and 2023. Last year Crystal Palace beat Liverpool and ended up finishing 15th, although they did go on to win the Conference League. The Reds also had a disappointing domestic campaign, finishing fifth. Some 47% of the time (16/34) the upcoming season's Premier League winners had not been involved in the Community Shield - like Arsenal in 2025-26. And 53% of the time (18/34) the Shield winners have finished above the losers in the league that season. On 10 occasions the two teams have finished as the top two in the Premier League - with four of those times being the Shield winners top and the losers as runners-up. The other question is how many Community Shields are won by the previous season's Premier League winners. But in recent times it has become less frequent. Including Crystal Palace, the FA Cup winners have won eight of the past 12 Shields, something that had only happened five times in the previous 22. And on three occasions in the Premier League era, neither the league nor cup winners have won it. Arsenal (1999 and 2023) and Manchester United (2010) qualified as Premier League runners-up and beat the Double winners in the game. Cole Palmer's breakthrough season came after his 2023 Community Shield goal - albeit for a different club Crystal Palace's 2025 scorers Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr netted 37 goals between them last season. Hugo Ekitike scored his first of 17 goals in his debut season for Liverpool - but Jeremie Frimpong did not enjoy a great first campaign after netting. In 2023 Cole Palmer netted for Manchester City in their game against Arsenal (a match they would go on to lose on penalties after Leandro Trossard's injury-time equaliser). He would go on to score 22 Premier League goals and be named young player of the season... for Chelsea, having joined them for £42.5m. The previous season, Darwin Nunez scored on his Liverpool debut - and Erling Haaland failed to notch on his City bow. That led to post-match discussion about Nunez looking the better player. However, Haaland went on to 52 goals that season, with Nunez netting only 15. Kelechi Iheanacho only scored four Premier League goals after his 2021 Community Shield winner. But back in 2019 Raheem Sterling's Shield strike for City against former club Liverpool kick-started the most productive season of his career (31 goals). Breton of Randolph, Maine, passed away peacefully on Aug. 13, 2026, leaving behind a legacy of faith, family, friendship, service, and adventure. Born on April 11, 1950, in Augusta, Richard lived a life rich with purpose and filled with the people and passions he loved most. After graduating from Cony High School, Dick married his high school sweetheart. In 1969, he joined the Army National Guard, where he proudly served for six years. He built a successful career in the grocery industry, beginning at Mister Market. He later joined Cottle’s Supermarket, working his way up to Store Manager, and continued his career with the company—now known as Hannaford—for 38 years. Dick enjoyed camping with his three daughters and, later, with his six grandchildren. He loved traveling with his wife and their special friends, and he especially cherished riding his Harley. He looked forward each year to motorcycle trips with his nephew Randy and their group of riders who affectionately called themselves the “Mild Hogs.” A man of deep faith, Richard was a member of St. Michael’s Parish in Augusta and a former choir member at St. Augustine Church. His lifelong love of music brought joy to his life and to all who knew him. He was a member of the Augusta Rotary Club for 13 years and served as President for one year. He especially enjoyed playing Santa at the annual Rotary Children’s Christmas Party. Richard was also a member of the Knights of Columbus Abnaki Council #334 and Le Club Calumet, and he served on the Festival de la Bastille committee for several years. During the Christmas season, he found great fulfillment in ringing the bell for the Salvation Army. Richard maintained an active lifestyle throughout his life. He enjoyed tennis, pickleball, golf, and kayaking adventures with the love of his life, Linette. Together, these snowbirds created countless treasured memories in both Maine and Florida. Dick was predeceased by his parents, Napoleon and Florence Breton; sisters Theresa Tardiff, Anita Martin and Yvette Breton, and brother, Eugene “Blackie” Breton. Above all, Richard was a devoted family man. He is survived by his wife of 57 years, Linette; his three daughters, Christine Devine (Christopher), Amy Perkins (Fred), and Allison Gallagher (Ron); his sister, Pauline Pelton; and his beloved grandchildren, Derek (and his wife Kayleigh), Jordan, Kyle, Nate, Casey, and Megan. One of Richard’s greatest joys was spending time with his grandchildren. He was also blessed to be a great-grandfather to Oliver and Remy. Richard celebrated each milestone of his growing family with love and unwavering support. He will be remembered for his warm smile, generous spirit, and his gift for making everyone feel welcomed and valued. To Richard, no one was ever a stranger. His memory will forever be cherished by his family and friends. A Mass of Christian Burial and celebration of Richard’s life will be held on Friday, Aug. 21 at 10 a.m. at St. Augustine Catholic Church, 75 Northern Ave., Augusta. Interment will follow at Holy Family Cemetery. The family would like to extend heartfelt gratitude to the staff at Andwell Hospice House for the support and kindness shown during this difficult time. Arrangements have been entrusted to Plummer Funeral Home, 16 Pleasant St., Augusta. title: Is Liverpool v Como on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch pre-season friendly - Yahoo Sports
content: Liverpool get their final tune-up before the Premier League season gets underway as they host Champions League-bound Como at Anfield. The Reds will face the Italian team twice in the same day, with the first clash kicking off in the morning behind closed doors before the fan element is introduced for the evening meeting. Andoni Iraola will be hoping for better fortunes after his losing Anfield bow, which saw Liverpool throw away another 2-0 lead to suffer a late 3-2 defeat to AS Monaco last weekend. Cesc Fabregas' Como, meanwhile, will look to go better than their spirited draw against Arsenal last time out. Liverpool's pre-season clash with Como kicks off at 6pm BST on Sunday 16 August at Anfield. The behind-closed-doors meeting kicks off at 11:30am BST. Fans can watch both games on All Red Video, Liverpool's club streaming platform. Jeremy Jacquet could be in line for his Liverpool debut after spending all of pre-season so far working up to match fitness following a knee injury last term. Alexis Mac Allister may return after coming back from his post-World Cup break, while Curtis Jones is also in contention after a hip issue. Joe Gomez is out injured. Como could hand Trevoh Chalobah a first start after making his debut off the bench against Arsenal. Liverpool XI: Alisson; Frimpong, Ndukwe, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Szoboszlai, Gravenberch; Elliott, Wirtz, Gakpo; Isak. Como XI: Butez; Couto, Chalobah, Kempf, Valle; De Cunha, Perrone; Liberali, Baturina, Diao; Douvikas.

title: BTS' V's hearing loss, K-Dramas smash ratings records, TXT's Yeonjun conquers LA: This week in K-Entertainment - Gulf News
content: Record-breaking K-dramas, Grammy backlash and BTS health scares shake K-pop Korea's entertainment machine never idles, but this week it downright sprinted. Four dramas raced ahead in ratings, the Grammys got a very public case of cold feet, a TXT member played the Troubadour like it was no big deal, and two-thirds of BTS opened their hearts to ARMY. Nielsen Korea had a busy Sunday. KBS 2TV's freshman drama Love on the Menu cracked the 15 percent ceiling for the first time, with its sixth episode pulling a 15.1 percent nationwide average, enough to make it the single most-watched program of the night, any genre, any channel. Meanwhile, The Husband went out on top: its series finale scored 8.5 percent, its best number of the entire run. Over on cable, tvN's Spooky in Love ghosted its own previous high, climbing to 6.2 percent, while JTBC's "The Apartment Job" matched the energy with a personal-best 6.1 percent as it heads into its final week. Four shows, four records, one very good night to own a TV ratings license in Korea. Remember the new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category the Recording Academy unveiled back in June? BTS declined to submit their new album ARIRANG, and the fallout is still rippling a month later. Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. broke his silence this past Saturday, acknowledging that some artists feel the new category doesn't represent their work the way they'd hoped, and that the Academy is committed to making adjustments so artists feel genuinely represented. It's a diplomatic way of saying: yes, we noticed, and yes, it stings. For context, the category covers K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop based on language rather than an artist's nationality. BTS, for their part, posted on Instagram expressing hope that their music could be appreciated on its own terms rather than sorted by region or language. The group has picked up five Grammy nods since 2021, mostly in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, so this isn't a case of sour grapes; it's a genuine philosophical disagreement about how their music should be judged. Submissions for the 2027 Grammys close August 21, with nominations landing November 16 and the ceremony set for February 7, 2027, at Crypto.com Arena. TXT's Yeonjun spent Wednesday night doing something that tends to only happen to genuine stars: Headlining the Troubadour in Los Angeles, the same room that hosted Elton John's US debut in 1970, Harry Styles' first solo show in 2017, and BTS's earliest American concert back in 2014. As part of Billboard's One Night Only series, Yeonjun ran through cuts from his No Labels: Part 02 EP, debuted a live performance of the explicit version of his song and closed with an encore of a solo mixtape track. The concert capped a genuinely stacked American run, Yeonjun became only the second Korean solo act (after BTS's Jungkook) to perform on Good Morning America's Summer Concert Series, and the first Korean artist tapped for Z100's Summer Bash. He wasn't done yet, either: the "Fxxking Star" music video dropped Thursday, followed by a ceremonial first pitch at Dodger Stadium for Korean Heritage Night. Efficient week. The rather heavy story of the week came out of a Weverse Live, where V and Jungkook talked about injuries they'd mostly kept to themselves. V revealed he's been dealing with hearing loss in one ear for roughly two and a half years, describing his affected ear as functioning at around 30 percent compared to a fully healthy ear, and admitted the issue actually started during his military service, where the culture around him initially framed it as a willpower problem rather than a medical one. He's now prioritising regular hospital visits and says fatigue has crept into recent shows, occasionally holding him back from performing at full intensity. Jungkook matched the candor, revealing his shin is sitting right on the edge of a stress fracture, with doctors noting significant inflammation after a recent hospital visit. Both members essentially asked fans for the same thing: patience, as a packed touring schedule doesn't leave much room to actually heal. title: Starship's 33 engines push down with 74,400 kilonewtons at liftoff — roughly twice the force of the Saturn V that sent humans to the Moon, yet the whole vehicle is designed to be caught like a falling pencil and flown again the next day - Space Daily
content: SpaceX's bet is that catching and reusing a 5,000-tonne rocket is cheaper than building a new one, and the engineering challenges of making that work may matter far more than raw horsepower. At the moment of liftoff, SpaceX’s Starship pushes off the launch pad with approximately 74.4 million newtons of thrust — enough force, in principle, to lift roughly 7,500 tonnes of mass directly against gravity. For context, that is about twice the thrust of the Saturn V rocket that carried the Apollo astronauts to the Moon between 1969 and 1972. The vehicle itself is taller — 121 metres compared to Saturn V’s 111 — and heavier when fully fuelled, with a total mass at liftoff exceeding 5,000 tonnes. By raw physical output, Starship is the most powerful rocket ever built. But raw thrust is not really the point of Starship. Saturn V hit similar physical scales half a century ago. What Starship is actually attempting to prove — and what its engineering choices really reflect — is not the maximum size of a rocket. It is the maximum turnaround time between launches. If it works, that is the innovation that changes what humans can do in space. The Super Heavy booster — the massive first stage of Starship — is powered by 33 Raptor 2 engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Each Raptor 2 produces approximately 2,260 kilonewtons of thrust at sea level, roughly 230 tonnes-force. Multiplied across 33 engines, the total is about 74.4 million newtons, or 16.7 million pounds-force. This is more than the current maximum thrust of NASA’s Space Launch System (about 39,144 kilonewtons) and more than double that of the Saturn V (about 35,000 kilonewtons). The rocket burns through propellant at an extraordinary rate. Super Heavy contains 3,400 tonnes of liquid methane and liquid oxygen. All 33 engines burn continuously for approximately 166 seconds during the first stage of ascent, consuming roughly 20 tonnes of propellant per second at peak flow. At that point, the second stage — the Starship spacecraft itself — separates and continues to orbit under its own six Raptor engines, while the Super Heavy booster reverses course and returns to the launch site. That return is where the specific engineering revolution actually lives. Saturn V was, by any measure, an extraordinary rocket. It launched 13 times between 1967 and 1973. Every one of those launches ended with the entire rocket falling into the ocean, breaking apart, or burning up. Not a single Saturn V was ever recovered, refurbished, or flown again. Every subsequent large rocket, until roughly 2015, followed the same pattern. Rockets were manufactured, flown once, and discarded. A typical expendable launch cost hundreds of millions of dollars for a single flight, with essentially all of that expense written off the moment the rocket left the pad. SpaceX’s earlier Falcon 9 rocket began changing that pattern in 2015 by recovering and reusing its first stage — landing propulsively on a barge or landing pad and being refurbished for subsequent flights. Falcon 9 first stages have now flown as many as 20 times each, dropping the effective cost per launch substantially. Starship pushes the reusability logic further. Both stages — the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft — are designed to return to Earth and be reused. And the specific mechanism by which the booster returns is one of the strangest engineering choices in modern spaceflight. Instead of landing on legs, the Super Heavy booster returns to its launch site and is caught in mid-air by two enormous mechanical arms mounted on the launch tower. The arms are officially called “Mechazilla.” Everyone calls them the chopsticks. The specific reason for the choice is engineering economy. Landing legs add weight to the booster. Weight subtracts from payload capacity. A booster caught by the tower does not need to carry its own landing gear, which means every kilogram of tower catch mechanism is a kilogram less that the booster has to lift on every flight for the rest of its operational life. The catch itself is precise. The booster returns from space at hypersonic speeds, decelerates using its own engines during a landing burn, and hovers briefly near the tower before the arms close around it and grip specific hard points on the vehicle’s outer hull. The whole approach and catch typically takes less than a minute. SpaceX first successfully caught a returning Super Heavy on October 13, 2024, during flight test IFT-5. A second successful catch followed on March 6, 2025, during IFT-8. A third has since been achieved. The technique is not routine yet, but it has been demonstrated to work. The specific reason all of this matters is not that catching rockets is cool. It is that it makes rockets economically comparable to airplanes. An airplane costs a lot of money to build, but it flies thousands of times over its operational life. That is what makes air travel affordable. A rocket, historically, costs about the same as an airplane per unit but flies exactly once. That is why sending anything to orbit has always been extraordinarily expensive. If Starship can be caught, refurbished, and flown again within days rather than months, the per-flight cost drops by orders of magnitude. SpaceX’s stated design target is a full stack turnaround measured in hours to a few days, with the same booster potentially flying multiple times per week at full operational cadence. Whether SpaceX will actually hit that target is genuinely uncertain. The technology has not yet demonstrated it. As of the most recent test flight in May 2026, individual boosters have not been re-flown from a catch. The company continues to work through the specific engineering problems — thermal fatigue, structural stress, hardware refurbishment — that separate a caught booster from a re-launched one. But the framework is now in place. A rocket has been built that can produce twice the thrust of Saturn V and be caught back at the launch tower like an oversized bird returning to its perch. Whether the same rocket will be launching again within 24 hours is the question the next few years of Starship development are entirely about. If the answer turns out to be yes, the economics of everything else in spaceflight will change. Sending humans to Mars, refuelling spacecraft in orbit, building lunar bases — all of these become possible in ways that expendable rockets could never have supported. The 74 million newtons of thrust is the specific engineering credential that makes Starship serious. The catch-and-refly system is what makes it revolutionary. What still remains to be proven is whether the tower can catch what it catches, and let it go again, quickly enough to actually matter. title: What’s For Dinner? v. 21.07: It’s Pepper Season! Braised pork with peppers, Swordfish with red pepper aioli, and more… - Daily Kos
content:
This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to
			publication. A few Christmases ago some foodie friends sent us a very nice Italian cookbook (see below), with a note in the front about their favorite recipe in the book. It quickly became a favorite of ours, too. It features a mix of peppers – sweet and spicy – so I decided August would be a relevant time to present this recipe along with a couple other things we love to do with peppers. This makes a good dinner for two plus leftovers, and I have always found I haven’t left enough peppers for the second time, so consider increasing the amount (weighed, one time, at 14 oz after coring and trimming and all). We have cooked with the peppers we have, not the specific ones the recipe wants us to have, which we have not yet hunted down. I serve this over soft polenta, pouring/spreading the extra polenta onto a small, oiled tray to chill and fry up the next day. The book in fact suggests making the pork and peppers a day ahead and reheating to bubbling. We have never considered waiting that long 😉 Chop the onion, rosemary, garlic, and anchovies together into 1/4-inch pieces. Coat a 12″ skillet lightly with EVOO and heat over med-high, then add the peppers, plus salt and freshly ground black pepper. Toss lightly to sear for about 2 minutes, then remove. Add a bit more oil to that in the pan, and when it is hot, add the pork, salt and pepper it, and brown well on all sides for about 10 minutes, taking care that “the glaze on the bottom of the pan” does not burn. Halfway through, add the bay, and a minute or two later, the chopped onion mixture, and finish browning the pork over medium heat, making sure to stir enough that the garlic does not burn, while the onion becomes golden brown. Add the vinegar. Simmer it “down to nothing” while scraping up the glaze from the pan. Add back the peppers, plus the water and tomatoes. Adjust the heat and let the liquid bubble slowly, covered, 50 minutes or till the pork is tender, stirring occasionally. Check the seasoning and serve, or refrigerate overnight and reheat to bubbling the next day. Serving over soft polenta is recommended. This is from The Italian Country Table, by Lynne Rossetto Kasper I love grilling/roasting peppers! Red sweet peppers are especially good roasted. You can buy jarred, roasted red peppers if you do not have a grill, but you can also roast them in the oven, I am told, or under a broiler – but not too close. The important thing when roasting your own peppers is to roast them whole, turning as each side gets blackened (just the skin, not the flesh). All the time the peppers spend in the hot oven or over the grill (covered!) the whole peppers are roasting, and this time is essential for them to be done right. Then you put the peppers into a heat-resistant container, where they will sort of steam themselves for about 15 minutes. After that, rub off the outer skins, seed and stem the peppers, and you have a delicacy on your hands. Place in a food processor two medium red peppers roasted as above, peeled, stemmed, and seeded, with 1 Tbsp olive oil and about 3/4 tsp salt [original: 1 tsp – my notes say too much; YMMV depending on your use of the sauce.] This recipe is infinitely useful, but it has a specific origin in Weber’s book Real Grilling, in a recipe called “Eggplant, Prosciutto, and Mozzarella ‘Sandwiches’.” You grill oiled, half-inch-thick slices from a globe eggplant – two per “sandwich” – one on both sides till done (maybe 4 minutes on a side on medium) and the other only on its first side. Turn the half-done slice so it is uncooked-side down, top with a Tbsp [or more] red pepper sauce, then a folded slice of prosciutto, a slice of fresh mozzarella, and then basil and the doubly-cooked eggplant on top. Grill, covered, till the bottom eggplant is fully cooked and the cheese is softened. With your food processor running, drop in two roughly chopped garlic cloves and run till minced. Add two red peppers, as above, grilled, peeled, stemmed and seeded, plus 3 Tbsp fresh lemon juice. Puree. In a small bowl, combine the puree with 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/4 tsp Kosher salt, and a pinch of cayenne pepper. Keep refrigerated if you’re not using it immediately, but return to room temperature for the recipe that follows. This aioli recipe is from Weber’s Art of the Grill, in a recipe called “Swordfish Kabobs with Roasted Red Pepper Aioli.” OMG this is so good. One probably both cannot and should not have it often, due to the price and possible mercury accumulation in swordfish, but as an occasional treat, perhaps one could be forgiven. The original recipe is for 2 pounds skinless swordfish, which is a lot – my notes say 1 lb worked for three of us. So I make half the recipe and serve any leftovers for lunch the next day. These are the original amounts, for 2 lb fish. Cut the swordfish into 1 1/2″ cubes, and marinate in the refrigerator for 30 minutes in a mixture of 3 Tbsp olive oil, 2 Tbsp freshly squeezed lemon juice, 1 Tbsp paprika (“preferably Hungarian”), and 1 tsp each chili powder and Kosher salt. Skewer the swordfish and grill over direct, medium heat, turning occasionally, until just opaque, about 5-6 minutes total (covered, always). My notes say, “Jasmine rice went with it perfectly!” The fish is excellent on its own, and so we served it to my father-in-law, who hated peppers, suggesting he try the aioli. He marveled to himself that he was going back for seconds of peppers! You’re getting all my favorite cookbooks in this diary (well, not all, they wouldn’t fit). This is from Pintxos, by Gerald Hirigoyen. Piperade is the kind of all-purpose recipe relegated to the “ingredients” section in the back of the book. Slice one small onion thinly, lengthwise. Core, seed, and cut into lengthwise strips 1 red and 1 yellow sweet pepper. Thickly slice (or crush) 6 peeled garlic cloves. Core and cut into ~ 3/4″ cubes four ripe tomatoes (I measured this to be about a pound). I use my monster 12″ Revere frying pan for this. Heat the pan over med-high, then add 1/3 cup olive oil and when it ripples, add the onion, peppers, garlic, and tomatoes. Cook for about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally (or more often) “until the vegetables have softened and have begun to color.” Remove from the heat and allow to cool, then stir in Piment d’Espelette – my notes say 1 tsp worked – and Kosher salt, perhaps a generous version of 1/2 tsp. This stores in the fridge up to 5 days. First off, this works just as a condiment beside an omelette, sausage, good cheese, meat or fish, or whatever you like. Omelette: Mr pixxer cooked up three eggs with a bit of milk, S&P, then added raclette (a great melty cheese) and at the end, some piperade. He jerks the pan to flip over the omelette. I have never been that brave. Pizza! I tried using up leftover piperade once in a pizza, and I loved it. Mixed mozzarella and parmiggiano, more of the former than the latter, put 2/3 of it onto a slightly pre-baked pizza crust, spread piperade over it, and topped with the rest of the cheese. Easy! Sandwich: Just put it on a sandwich with cheese or whatever else you make sandwiches with. Not peanut butter. Piperade-braised beans with baked eggs: This is a classic, and the recipe is originally from Pintxos. Using the 3 cups (one recipe) of piperade above, 2 cups chicken or veal stock, and 2 cups dried cannellini beans (picked over, rinsed, soaked, drained), plus a 2-oz piece of smoked ham, and two choricero peppers (YMMV – I have not found this particular type), cook the beans for 1 or 1 1/2 hours, or till tender but not mushy. The chef has you discard the ham and choricero peppers but I would for sure eat the ham 🙂 Let cool to “warm”* and preheat the oven to 400. This is enough for six servings, but we make only two of the following, and have the rest reheated later without the eggs. Fill oven proof dishes each with about 1/6 of the bean mixture, make a well in the center of each, and break an egg into it. Place on a rimmed baking sheet or on the oven rack if you are confident you will not spill anything. Cook about 15 minutes, or until the whites are cooked, but the yolks are still soft. Sprinkle with salt and some parsley and serve. [*I have found that you need the beans pretty warm for the egg to cook effectively in them. The beans will be either insulating or cooking the bottom of the eggs.] Here’s one last, lovely pepper recipe from Martha Stewart. This is a GREAT potluck dish in that it’s easy to mix at the last minute. Opposing that…. well, if the definition of “gift item” is “something that looks more expensive than it is,” perhaps the definition of “potluck contribution” should be “something that looks harder than it is.” This is not that, simply b/c it takes a lot of time to cut everything carefully.
