title: Jaguars training camp stock report after first preseason game v. Saints - Yahoo Sports
content: The Jacksonville Jaguars have wrapped up their first preseason game of 2026, defeating the New Orleans Saints on the road by a score of 24 to 20. With the dust now having settled, let's take stock of where this team stands, with a look at those who are on the rise and those who dropped. The yards often didn't come easy, but Taylor found ways to steadily churn out positive gains. He played key roles in the Jaguars moving the ball down the field during their two second-half scoring drives. He finished the game with 78 yards on 22 carries with a touchdown. This is a position group already dealing with numerous injuries, and then Chuma Edoga exited the game on the first play. Also sidelined coming into this game were Walker Little and Patrick Mekari. Cole Van Lanen remains on the PUP list. Down Edoga and with the backups in, the offensive line unit took its lumps in this game. Coming into the training camp, the depth behind Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker was a big question mark, but the rotational members of this unit have performed well this summer, and that continued in Saturday's game. Danny Striggow had three tackles, half a sack, and a quarterback hit. BJ Green had a fumble recovery, with help from Wesley Williams on that play. Williams also showcased that well-rounded skill set that the coaches have talked about. Saints' quarterback Zach Wilson averaged 9.1 yards per attempt on 16 passes, generating several explosive plays through the air, at least two of which had Ballentine as the nearest defender. When in the game, Abdullah seemed to be all over the field. He finished with two tackles, including one for a loss, a sack, and a quarterback hit. He also helped create the disruption that led to the fumble by Spencer Rattler. It's the preseason -- wins and losses don't matter. Also, the starters did not play in this contest either. That said, Coen wants to build a resilient team that fights to the end, and this Jaguars' roster did that, scoring 18 straight points in the second half to win the game. title: Cadillac unveils V-One Concept Hypercar for the street - The Detroit News
content: Here’s a stoplight drag race we’d like to see at a future Woodward Dream Cruise: the Porsche 963 RSP vs. the Cadillac V-One. At Carmel, California’s summer autopalooza last week, The Quail, General Motor’s luxury brand unveiled the wicked-looking V-One Concept based on the Cadillac V-Series.R Hypercar that endurance races across the globe from Daytona to Le Mans. The V-One comes a little over a year after Porsche’s street-legal hypercar — also based on their Le Mans endurance racer — debuted at the 2025 24 Hours of Le Mans in France. The car was gifted by Porsche to Roger Penske, Porsche’s partner in international sports car racing. Like the 963 RSP (short for Roger Searle Penske), the V-One is a street-focused version of the V-Series.R. The two cars are likely the fastest street-legal vehicles ever conceived. Unlike the Porsche, Cadillac hailed the V-One as a halo for future V-Series brand design. “The Cadillac V-One Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Global Cadillac Executive Design Director Dominic Najafi before the silk was pulled off the new Caddy. Development of a production car from a race car is hardly new at GM. The current Corvette C8 Z06, for example, was developed alongside the Corvette GT3.R race car that also competes in international sportscar racing. The Z06 shares the same, high-revving, dual-overhead can V-8 engine as the race car. Unlike the Corvette, however, which sells 25-35,000 units a year, the V-One Concept would be a rare vehicle if produced. “It’s about as close to the race car as you can get,” says Sean O’Shea, Cadillac Hypercar Propulsion Manager. V-One is a notable departure from recent Cadillac concepts that had electric powertrains (the Opulent Velocity, Solleim and InnerSPace). The addition of the V-One to Cadillac’s halo arsenal alongside those concepts and the hand-built Celestiq EV indicates the continued co-existence of electric and V-8s within the brand. Not only does V-One boast an eight-cylinder engine prized by Dream Cruisers like the CT5 V-Series Blackwing road car — but it is also a hybrid. Cadillac does not sell a hybrid vehicle. “At the heart of the V-One is a V-8 hybrid powertrain that shares foundations with the Cadillac V-Series.R race car, underscoring the concept’s serious capability and authenticity,” said the Cadillac press release of the electrified, 5.5-liter V-8. Under 37 mph, the race car operates on the electric motor before the V-8 roars to life leaving the pit lane. That duality is likely shared by the V-One. While V-One shares the race car’s earth-shaking powertrain, it possesses significantly more power: 830-horsepower versus 670 for the V-Series.R due to so-called Balance of Performance racing regulations to encourage close racing between brands as varied as Cadillac, Porsche, Ferrari, BMW, Aston Martin, etc that compete in Hyeprcar racing with their own production-derived powerplants. That is also true of the Corvette Z06 which produces 670 horsepower (the highest of any normally-aspirated production car) versus 500 for the GT3.R. Other elements of the V-One closely track the race car including its carbon-fiber monocoque chassis made by the Dallara race shop in Italy, high-downforce aerodynamics, and sophisticated suspension. They also appear to share track-focused Michelin Pilot Sport slicks. Where the V-One departs from its sibling is in its premium detailing — notably a striking silver-to-night paint job (the race car gets a vinyl wrap) and luxurious cockpit materials. The interior is made with recycle materials, carbon-fiber trim, and a more comfortable driver’s seat (while still holding the driver in at a neck-straining 3 Gs at, ahem, 150 mph). The steering wheel is less complicated and bears a screen. “The interior of the car is one of the main selling points with the car," said O’Shea. “You open the doors and you look inside and it's a clean, purpose-built race car with a bespoke Cadillac interior.” The intention to make the car more utilitarian (the V-One engine, assures Cadillac, doesn’t require “a team of specialists just to operate”), but its track roots are still a priority. Cadillac says, despite the added luxury and weight, V-One should lap withing 10% of V-Series.R times. A serialized plaque on the door teases Cadillac’s intention to make more copies for sale. Perhaps as a garage partner to the also- limited edition, hand-built Celestiq EV. “(V-One) is a serious machine, but it’s amazing how we’ve been able to bring this curated design element to it to make it feel like a very special car,” said Nafaji. “The Celestiq represents ultimate luxury, the V-One represents ultimate performance.” Henry Payne is auto critic for The Detroit News. title: Sergio V. Crowley Publishes Operations Research Framework for Industrial Capital Deployment - markets.businessinsider.com
content:
"The Physics of Capital" applies engineering-grade precision to corporate asset allocation, with detailed application to agriculture drone economics. United States, August 15, 2026 -- Most corporate capital allocation still runs on spreadsheets built from assumptions. Industry averages. Competitor benchmarks. Projections that feel reasonable but connect loosely to the actual hardware sitting in the field. Sergio V. Crowley wrote "The Physics of Capital" because he thinks that approach destroys value in ways executives rarely trace back to its source. The book, published by ENGI Products LLC, presents what Crowley calls an Operations Research Command Framework. The methodology treats capital decisions the way engineers treat load calculations. Inputs come from measurable variables. Outputs follow deterministic logic. Guesswork gets replaced by data. "Capital efficiency in modern industry cannot be sustained through qualitative speculation or abstract management theories," Crowley said. "True strategic control demands treating corporate resources with the exact mathematical precision and deterministic laws that govern the mechanical properties of materials." At the center sits a formula: Kₛ = (i × Φ × τ × Ω) ÷ TCO Capital stability, in Crowley's framework, emerges from the interaction between initial investment, operational variables, time horizons, degradation factors, and total cost of ownership. The equation gives executives something concrete to calculate rather than estimate. Plug in the numbers. See what comes out. Adjust the inputs until the output makes sense for the organization's liquidity position. The book applies this framework to precision agriculture drones. Specifically, drones configured with liquid sprayer systems. Crowley excludes granular fertilization applications entirely. The distinction matters because liquid sprayers create different stress profiles on airframes, drain batteries at different rates, and require maintenance on different schedules. Treating all agricultural drones as interchangeable in financial models introduces error that compounds over fleet lifecycles. Battery degradation gets its own extended analysis. How many charge cycles before capacity drops below operational thresholds? What does temperature exposure during summer field operations do to that timeline? How does seasonal usage, heavy in growing months and light otherwise, affect the math? Crowley argues that most asset planning underweights these variables, leading organizations to misattribute capital erosion to factors they cannot control when the real cause sits in their own modeling assumptions. "When deploying high-precision autonomous systems, such as agriculture drones utilizing liquid sprayers exclusively, operational success requires isolating financial metrics from generic planning," Crowley said. "By anchoring decisions strictly in Total Cost of Ownership and empirical hardware variables, we eliminate financial friction and protect corporate liquidity." The framework extends beyond agriculture. Manufacturing robotics. Logistics automation. Infrastructure maintenance equipment. Any context where expensive hardware operates under variable conditions, degrades on predictable curves, and requires replacement decisions that span multiple budget cycles. The math transfers. The inputs change. The logic stays the same. CAPEX and OPEX show up throughout the book as interdependent rather than separate line items. What an organization spends upfront affects what it spends annually. What it spends annually shapes when and how much it needs to reinvest. Crowley maps these feedback loops explicitly. Traditional budgeting tends to treat capital expenditure and operational expenditure as distinct planning exercises. The framework rejects that separation. Industrial Asset Lifecycle Management runs through every chapter. Crowley traces equipment from acquisition through deployment, performance decay, maintenance intervention, and eventual replacement. Financial modeling at each stage allows treasury and operations teams to anticipate liquidity requirements months or years before they hit. The alternative, reacting to degradation as it happens, leaves organizations perpetually behind their own cash flow needs. For operations directors and CFOs evaluating autonomous system deployments, the practical value is straightforward. Stop building allocation models from averages. Start building them from the specifications of the actual equipment, the actual environmental conditions, and the actual degradation data available from vendors or historical operations. The formula provides the structure. The variables come from reality rather than assumption. Corporate governance literature has moved toward quantitative rigor in recent years. Boards increasingly expect capital allocation frameworks that can be audited, tested, and revised as conditions change. Crowley's methodology fits that expectation. Every input is traceable. Every output follows from documented calculation. Disagreements become debates about data rather than intuition. The book targets executive leadership, operations directors, and financial officers making capital decisions in hardware-intensive environments. Technical depth is substantial but accessible to readers with basic financial modeling familiarity. The precision agriculture examples ground abstract concepts in operational reality that translates across sectors. The hardcover edition is available through Amazon, and so is the paperback edition. title: Cadillac’s 830-HP V-ONE is its wildest performance concept in 20 years - How-To Geek
content: Cadillac hasn't built a true one-off concept since the Cien debuted at the 2002 Detroit Auto Show, a drivable V12 supercar that hinted at where Cadillac's performance ambitions were headed, right up until the cost of its custom engine and a projected $200,000 price tag kept it from ever reaching production. The V-ONE picks up that same thread, except this time the concept isn't just inspired by racing. It's built from it. Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and chassis builder Dallara developed the V-ONE together. The single-seat concept shares its suspension, transmission, and hybrid V8 foundation with the V-Series.R, the prototype winning races at Le Mans and across the IMSA and WEC calendars since 2023. Plenty of automakers start with a production platform, add a wing, wheels, and graphics, and call the result track-inspired. Cadillac did the total opposite with the V-ONE, starting with actual competition hardware and working from there to build something a single owner could eventually sit in and drive. Although the V-ONE won’t be for sale, what Cadillac is showing here with its debut at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering, is where the V-Series line could head next. As noted a moment ago, the V-ONE shares its foundation with the Cadillac V-Series.R, the prototype that competes in the IMSA WeatherTech Championship and the FIA World Endurance Championship. Since the V-Series.R debuted in 2023, Cadillac Racing has picked up 10 wins, 16 pole positions, and 32 podiums across IMSA and WEC competition. The stretch includes the 2023 IMSA WeatherTech Championship sweep of the manufacturer, team, and driver titles, a front-row Hyperpole lockout at the 2025 24 Hours of Le Mans, and Cadillac's first 1-2 finish in WEC competition at São Paulo. The V-ONE concept's hybrid drivetrain shares its foundation with the V-Series.R race engine, delivering a combined output of 830 horsepower. The concept also uses the same double wishbone suspension setup as the V-Series.R, with pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements plus lateral and heave dampers front and rear. Meanwhile, the transmission and select electronics also carry over from the race car, while the aero package follows the same proportions that helped the V-Series.R compete at Le Mans and other WEC events. Cadillac's goal with the V-ONE is to keep that race-bred hardware intact while making the car easier and more intuitive for a single driver to operate. This monstrous machine leaves sports cars in its dust. Cadillac's V-Series performance lineage and the idea of a one-of-one build come together in the name V-ONE. Its single-seat cockpit is the first of its kind for the brand, which might be somewhat hard to believe given Cadillac’s racing heritage. Inside, the seat is shaped to the driver's exact measurements, while the steering wheel layout was created with race engineers for actual track use. Instead of a standard infotainment system, the V-ONE uses a race-inspired interface and data visualization system designed to give the driver feedback as they explore the car's limits. Other unique touches inside include recycled fabrics and exposed carbon. As for the exterior, the hand-sprayed paint features a gradient blend from silver to deep navy, meant to reflect the shift from day to night during an endurance race. The concept also gets a new V-Series wheel design, updated V-Series badging, and a serialized plaque on the door. Cadillac is channeling the energy of its racing programs into more than just wildly cool concepts like the V-ONE. To mark its first season on the Formula 1 grid, the automaker built just 26 units of the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series, a 685-horsepower, manual-transmission sedan developed alongside Formula 1 and the FIA. Likewise, Cadillac gave the F1 Collector Series the same kind of hands-on attention to detail as the V-ONE. Working with their colleagues at GM Motorsports, Cadillac engineers created the most powerful Blackwing to date. The 6.2-liter V8, which produces 685 horsepower and 673 lb-ft. of torque, has an upgraded supercharger with a CNC-machined cover and a laser-etched FIA logo, created in-house by GM Motorsports. Each of the 26 cars is finished in Midnight Stone Frost, a matte black paint that mirrors the Cadillac F1 Team livery. Noteworthy interior details include a 3D-printed F1 shifter medallion and a custom Cadillac Formula 1 door sill plate. Although the V-ONE is not for sale and the CT5-V Blackwing F1 Collector Series was extremely limited, both show the promise of the V-Series lineup. With the V-ONE especially, enthusiasts have a lot to look forward to. "The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future," said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. title: Chelsea v Real Sociedad | Match | Official Site - Chelsea Football Club
content: Morgan Rogers marked his first game in Chelsea colours with a goal and Joao Pedro added to his impressive summer tally by bagging a brace as Xabi Alonso’s Blues ended our pre-season schedule in style. On a sizzling summer’s afternoon in west London, Rogers poked us ahead early on after Joao Pedro’s header had been well saved. Sociedad carried a threat of their own and levelled shortly before the half-time whistle courtesy of Jon Mikel Aramburu’s fine volley. However, the second half was very much Chelsea’s, and our dominance was rewarded through a pair of Joao Pedro goals - his sixth and seventh of pre-season. The well-placed header that restored our lead arrived a couple of minutes into the second half, and the Brazilian backed that up by making a one-on-one opportunity look very easy as this enjoyable friendly entered its final act. Xabi Alonso, getting his first taste of the  home dugout at the Bridge, was able to give minutes to 20 of his players, including several who had yet to feature this pre-season. For the Blues fans watching on, it whet the appetite for what lies ahead, with the start of the Premier League campaign just over a week away now. Before kick-off, Alonso received a great ovation from the Chelsea supporters inside the stadium, and indeed the small pocket of travelling fans who saw him come through Real Sociedad’s ranks in the late nineties. Alonso’s first Stamford Bridge starting XI included new signings Marco Palestra, Maxence Lacroix and Rogers. The latter two were playing their first game for us having returned to training earlier in the week. The shape was nominally 3-4-3, with Pedro Neto and Palestra the wing-backs. Reece James joined Moises Caicedo in midfield, with Cole Palmer and Rogers – as well as Neto and Palestra – supporting Joao Pedro. It was apparent from the off how fluid the attack would be, with Joao Pedro regularly dropping deeper, allowing Rogers and Palmer to run beyond. However, it was from Joao Pedro’s positioning in a central striking position that we took the lead in the tenth minute. Neto teased a cross in from the right flank and the Brazilian’s header back across goal was well directed. Visiting keeper Alex Remiro, diving to his left, just reached it but succeeded only in teeing up Rogers, who couldn’t miss in front of the Shed. Joao Pedro almost immediately forced Remiro into another good save, with nobody in blue able to pick up the pieces on this occasion. Sociedad then threatened for the first time, Ander Barrenetxea cutting inside and curling a shot not far wide. Either side of a hydration break, which offered both teams some respite on another scorching London afternoon, Take Kubo shot into the side-netting and Rob Sanchez produced a superb reaction save to deny Jon Martin. It looked like we had quietened the Sociedad threat sufficiently before the break, but the side from San Sebastian equalised on the stroke of half-time through Arambaru’s brilliantly executed 20-yard volley. Sanchez stood no chance. The Blues came out of the blocks quickly and soon restored our lead, in similar fashion to the opener. Palmer twisted back and forth before laying the ball off for James to send over a right-wing cross. Joao Pedro rose highest and this time his header was steered beyond Remiro’s reach. Another attack involving Palmer ended with the Brazilian firing against Remiro’s legs as the angle narrowed, and there was plenty more slick interplay for the home fans to enjoy as we approached the hour mark. The first ranch of changes saw Mike Penders, Malo Gusto, Josh Acheampong and Enzo Fernandez enter the fray. Gusto went to right wing-back, with Neto switching to the left. One of Sociedad’s subs, Spain World Cup winner Mikel Oyarzabal, had a shot excellently blocked by Wesley Fofana shortly after coming on. But it was our leading man who was more decisive following another flurry of Blues subs – including a first sighting of Pep Chavarria in blue. Gusto played a fine through pass for Joao Pedro to run on to, and the confident finish that followed across Remiro felt inevitable. We continued to look threatening in the final quarter-hour, with Estevao shooting over and Jorrel Hato embarking on a lung-busting run from one end to the other that had the Blues fans roaring him on. It epitomised an enjoyable finale to pre-season. The Premier League season! The Blues begin the 2026/27 campaign by making the short trip to Craven Cottage to play Fulham next Monday 24 August. title: York City v Bristol Rovers: League Two stats & head-to-head - BBC
content: York City were playing their first match in the EFL since May 2016 York debutant Harry Boyes bagged a brace to mark the club's return to the English Football League after a 10-year absence with a thrilling 3-2 home triumph over Bristol Rovers. Boyes – a summer signing from Southend – netted the first EFL goals of his career and was joined on the Minstermen scoresheet by Alex Newby. Clinton Mola had given Steve Evans' visitors a first-half lead and substitute Tommy Leigh later levelled from the penalty spot, but Boyes had the last say for York. A raucous sell-out home crowd were quietened when the Pirates scored from their first attack on the half-hour mark. Keenan Gough's long ball picked out Fabrizio Cavegn on the left and his low cross saw Mola squeeze a shot goalkeeper Alfie McNally. York responded with two goals in four second-half minutes. First, on the hour, Joe Grey's low cross was turned in from eight yards by Newby before Boyes fired home from 15 yards in the 63rd minute. The visitors equalised in the 78th minute after Morgan Williams was controversially penalised for a shove and Leigh sent McNally the wrong way with the subsequent spot-kick. But Boyes headed in from a yard in the 80th minute to win it after Newby had nodded down Ollie Banks' deep cross. Evans: "It's individual errors for each of the goals" York City are winless in each of their last five Football League meetings with Bristol Rovers (D2 L3), since a 4-1 home win in 2012-13. The last time Bristol Rovers started a Football League campaign with an away trip to York City it ended goalless, in the 1971-72 third tier season in which the Gas finished sixth and the Minster Men 19th. This will be York’s first EFL game since a 1-1 draw with Morecambe in May 2016. Overall, they’ve won just one of their last 16 matches in the Football League (D5 L10), though did lose just one of their last six on home soil (W1 D4). Bristol Rovers ended the 2025-26 League Two campaign unbeaten in nine games (W8 D1) and they last went 10+ games unbeaten in the Football League between March and September 2007, a run of 13 ended by Yorkshire side Leeds United. title: Cadillac unveil V-Series.R based road concept - Motorsport Week
content: Cadillac reveals the new V-ONE Hypercar, a concept derived from proven race-winning machinery across both WEC and IMSA, the Cadillac V-Series.R. Rooted in the performance engineering shared with the Cadillac V-Series.R foundations, the V-ONE Concept explores how competition hardware can be translated into a driver-focused experience, while reinforcing Cadillac’s broader race-winning story across design, performance and technology. “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. The V-ONE is rooted in Cadillac’s LMDh racing program and informed by the V-Series.R race car, similar to Roger Penske’s Porsche 963 RS, based on the Porsche 963 LMDh, presented at the 24h of Le Mans in 2025. At the heart of the V-ONE is a V-8 hybrid powertrain that shares foundations with the Cadillac V-Series.R race car, underscoring the concept’s serious capability and authenticity. The concept also shares deeper race-bred architecture with the V-Series.R in areas such as suspension, transmission, and select electronics. Even with that race-derived foundation, the V-ONE is intended to be easier to operate while maintaining a similar level of performance. The V-ONE’s exterior remains faithful to the dramatic proportions and visual intent of the V-Series.R race car, while introducing refined details that make the concept feel more advanced and more technical. The Cadillac V-ONE Concept will be on display at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, California on August 14, 2026. And as confirmed, not for sale. title: Ranking the Best Bobby V Albums - Soul In Stereo
content: When you think of Bobby V(alentino), your mind probably goes two places – his mid 2000s run of radio singles (“Slow Down,” “Tell Me,” “Anonymous”) or his big features (“Pimpin All Over the World,” and, uggggggh, “Mrs. Officer”). But you may be surprised by how prolific Bobby V has been over the years. From his vastly underrated debut with R&B group Mista, aka the “Blackberry Molasses” boys, to a slew of EPs, mixtapes and LPs that spanned most of the 2010s, a film, and his current penchant for dropping random singles on Instagram, it seems like this man is always creating. So let’s do what we always do – look back at every LP, EP, and collab project he’s shared with us thus far, ranking them from bottom to top. Although we’re skipping mixtapes this time, I added a few surprises to make up for that. Edd said: So yeah, this was a thing. Bobby hit the small screen in 2016 with Hollywood Hearts, his acting debut. The project inevitably lead to a soundtrack, which served as an undercover Bobby V album. And …I have absolutely nothing to say about this. I’m not being facetious either – the production is marginal, the singing is OK, the writing is predictable. There’s absolutely nothing of note here, it’s just 44 minutes of content. No wonder I forgot this project existed. Edd said: Just six months after dropping his breakout solo debut, quietly Bobby V teamed with rapper STIX to hopefully improve upon Jay-Z and R. Kelly’s woeful Best of Both Worlds. They did not. The Next of Both Worlds serves up a handful of bland mid ’00s club tracks and OK-ish Radio&B. It’s much better when Valentino takes the lead but it still fails to impress. No shock that this one didn’t really go anywhere. Also, shouldn’t “Your My Girl” be “You’re My Girl?” Sheesh. Edd said: One listen to Dusk Till Dawn and you can tell that Bobby was long overdue for a refresh. Superproducers Tim & Bob – a constant presence on his early albums –  are limited to just one song here (one of the best songs, naturally). While he has a few fresh faces behind the boards, most just mimic the sounds that worked on previous projects. And it doesn’t help that the writing feels weaker this time around. Bobby needed a change at this point. Forgotten favorites: “Are You Ready,” “Ooh (She Got Me Like)” Edd said: I always felt like Fly on the Wall struggled to find an identity. We got four singles from this album – the most from any Bobby V project at this point – and none really stuck, with the slight exception of “Words.” The album was crammed with top tier production (Tim & Bob, Bryan-Michael Cox, Jazze Pha, Hit-Boy, Stevie J) and a ton of guests (50 Cent, Lloyd Banks, Twista, Plies – even Cyhi Da Prynce jumps off the back of a milk carton for this one). But between the excessive runtime and glut of songs that feel like “been there, done that,” Fly on the Wall can’t justify its buzz. Forgotten favorites: “Words,” “If I Can’t Have You” Edd said: It’s kinda wild that Bobby has gone almost a decade without an official studio project. Electrik works best when Bobby lingers in familiar territory. Tracks like “Lil Bit” and “Beautiful Life” feel like they were plucked from 2005 sessions with Tim and Bob. But despite solid attempts to return to form, several of the performances are too low energy. What should have been a strong comeback winds up too lethargic for its own good. His Static Shock album cover cosplay deserved better. Forgotten favorites: “Lil Bit,” “Promise U,” “Beautiful Life” Edd said: Following his split with Disturbing Tha Peace, Bobby returned with a slightly more mature outlook. The results are kinda weird – Tim & Bob are back behind the boards, with heavy hitters like Raphael Saadiq coming in clutch. Always a win. But despite all the ingredients being in place, the formula started to feel like it was losing its potency.  That could be due to the album’s erratic sequencing; reordering things would greatly help the album’s flow. Also, this is the project that gave us “Beep,” which only comes second to “Mrs. Officer” in the race for Most Annoying Song of the 2000s. There’s elements of a good album here, but it’s all over the place. Forgotten favorites: “Butterfly Tattoo,” “Just Me & You,” “My Girl” Edd said: By 2013, Bobby was ready for a change, and Peach Moon was part of that transition. This EP leans closer to jazzy soul than the hip-hop infused sounds and high-octane R&B that made Bobby a star, and it’s actually a solid fit. But at just six tracks, this feels more like a demo than a fleshed out project. Still, this had a ton of potential and I’d score it even higher if we got more. Neo-soul Valentino should have been a thing. Forgotten favorites: “Who Am I to Change,” “Koko Lovely,” “Never Give Up” Edd said: Bobby obviously has undeniable chemistry with Tim and Bob but Timbaland comes in at a very close second on Valentino’s sophomore album. “Anonymous” was a surefire hit and “Rearview (Ridin’)” was pretty fun too. I wish we got more of them together. But of course, Tim and Bob are back with the bangers as well, along with Dre & Vidal, Darkchild and others. The album starts quite strong with great midtempos and space-age sonics but it struggles to maintain the momentum on the second half. The loss of innovative tracks takes away from the fun. Without them, Special Occasion winds up a Typical Occasion. Forgotten favorites: “Rearview (Ridin’),” “Checkin’ For Me,” “Only Human” Edd said: Here’s another Bobby V EP you may have missed, and it’s the best one to date. Bobby teams with producer B Jabr, who laces Valentino was a very smooth, mellow sound. It’s what I’d imagine his group Mista would have evolved into in the 2000s. There are no big hits here, but it’s surprisingly fulfilling despite its extremely brief runtime. This was very impressive and I really wish he explored this sound later in his career when he was seeking direction. Forgotten favorites: “Another Life,” “What’s Going On” Edd said: I figured I’d throw in Bobby’s official introduction for a lil’ razzle dazzle. Mista stormed on the scene with a maturity that was leagues ahead of their young peers. Admittedly, the group was still rough around the edges vocally but the grit added to many of these emotional tracks. While the bluesy production couldn’t measure up to the flashy heavy-hitters of its era and the somber tone likely was too heavy for younger ears, Mista’s debut still was ahead of its time. I think we were robbed of something special with these guys. Forgotten favorites: “? (Heart) Is,” “Things You Do,” “Lady” Edd said: I’m pretty sure you all predicted which album would land on the top spot – sometimes, the most obvious answer is the most correct one. After a criminally overlooked run with Mista, Bobby Valentino linked up with battle-tested superproducers Tim and Bob to create R&B’s next great triple threat. “Slow Down” and “Tell Me” instantly became career defining singles and R&B had a new contender for the crown. But the album brought more to the table than those singles, thanks to the stellar production and catchy writing. This is the way to make a first impression and it’s still remembered as Bobby V’s defining work. …And 20 years later I’m STILL demanding a video for “Want You to Know Me.” Forgotten favorites: “Want You to Know Me,” “Never Lonely,” “One Girl to Love” What’s your favorite Bobby V album? Let us know below. Your email address will not be published. Required fields are marked * Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment.

title: BTS’ V Reveals He’s Receiving Treatment for Hearing Loss After Two-Year Battle - That Grape Juice.net
content: BTS member V has opened up about an ongoing health battle, revealing that he is receiving treatment for significant hearing loss in his right ear. Elizabeth V. Winnington, 80, of Garnet Valley, PA, died Wednesday, August 5, 2026, at her home surrounded by her family. A graduate of the University of Tennessee at Nashville and the University of Delaware, Beth worked as an Intensive Care Unit nurse and homemaker before finding her calling as a nurse paralegal for GEICO in Wilmington, Delaware. She was a committed member and Treasurer of Philanthropic Educational Organization (PEO), a non-profit organization providing scholarships, grants, awards, loans to women, especially those whose education has been interrupted and who find it necessary to return to school to complete a degree or certification. She was an avid reader and active member of two book clubs, one in her Belmont community and the other with her PEO sisters. She was also an active member of St. David’s Episcopal Church and its bible study group. She played an instrumental role in St. David’s outreach programs, including spearheading its support for Homeless Veterans and ensuring the success of its United Thank Offering. When not volunteering her time in support of her community, she enjoyed gardening and walking with each of her beloved dog companions through the years Beth was predeceased by her father Paul F. Winnington, her mother Elizabeth V. (Gibison), and siblings Frank Winnington and Mary Winnington. title: Cadillac Reveals V-ONE Concept Based on V-Series.R LMDh Car - Sportscar365
content: Cadillac takes wraps off concept prototype based on V-Series.R LMDh car… Cadillac has taken the wraps off its V-ONE prototype, billed as a concept study that “unites the Cadillac V-Series performance legacy with a one-of-one, single-seat expression” marking the first of its kind for the brand. Based on the Dallara-chassied V-Series.R LMDh car that competes in both the FIA World Endurance Championship and IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship, the V-ONE Concept was unveiled Friday at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, Calif., as part of Monterey Car Week. “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, Executive Design Director, Global Cadillac. The concept car, co-developed by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing and Dallara, is designed to deliver factory-level prototype performance and technology. The V8 hybrid powertrain shares foundations with the V-Series.R, but can produce an increased combined 830 horsepower, along with “race-bred” suspension, transmission and selected electronics from the LMDh car. Among other shared components include double wishbone suspension, pushrod-actuated coil and torsion spring elements with lateral and heave dampers on the front and rear. Additionally, the V-ONE Concept features an “intuitive, race-inspired interface and data visualization concept that gives drivers clear feedback and coaching as they explore the car’s full capability.” Cadillac has not made any indications of it plans to build and offer the car to customers, in what would most likely be for a track-day setting, similar to the Ferrari 499P Modificata and McLaren’s MCL-HY GTR. title: Cadillac V-One Turns Its Le Mans Racer Into an 830-HP Track Toy - Autoweek
content: The single-seat hybrid concept translates Cadillac’s IMSA and WEC prototype into a bespoke track-focused machine. The Cadillac V-One Concept, unveiled during Monterey Car Week, is a single-seat track car that draws directly from the V-Series.R prototype Cadillac races in both the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship and FIA World Endurance Championship. While Cadillac is calling the V-One a concept for now, the exercise suggests the automaker is looking at offering it to its wealthy customers, giving them, in essence, a factory-built track car with performance approaching that of its competition machinery. The V-One was developed jointly by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing, and Dallara, which builds the chassis for the V-Series.R. And it goes way beyond just replicating the race car’s look; the concept actually shares significant hardware with it, including elements of its suspension, transmission, electronics, and hybrid powertrain. That powertrain combines a V8 engine with hybrid assistance to produce 830 hp. Cadillac hasn’t released detailed performance figures, but the automaker says the V-One is intended to deliver performance comparable to the V-Series.R while being easier for a nonprofessional driver to operate. The suspension echoes the race car’s double-wishbone layout, pushrod-actuated springs, and separate lateral and heave dampers at both ends. Cadillac also gave it a race-inspired center screen that would give drivers with performance data and coaching as they learn the car. The connection to Cadillac’s racing program is more than cosmetic. Since debuting in 2023, the V-Series.R has tallied 10 victories, 16 pole positions, and 32 podium finishes across IMSA and WEC competition. Its résumé includes the 2023 IMSA manufacturers’, teams’, and drivers’ championships, the 2025 Le Mans Hyperpole, and Cadillac’s first WEC 1-2 finish at São Paulo. Visually, the V-One remains remarkably close to the competition car, retaining much of its basic body and proportions. It does sport new V-Series wheels and darkened badging, as well as a hand-painted gradient that transitions from silver to deep navy. Inside, there is room for only one. The exposed carbon-fiber cockpit gets a custom-fitted driver’s seat and a steering wheel whose button configuration can be tailored to the owner. Cadillac also incorporates more luxurious materials and a serialized plaque. Cadillac hasn’t announced production plans, pricing, or how many V-Ones it might build. The company describes it as the “ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept,” which leaves the door conspicuously open. A 2023 Chevrolet Bolt EV, 1972 VW Beetle, 2007 Porsche 911 Carrera S, and a well-loved purple-and-white five-speed Schwinn currently call her garage home. title: Cadillac Reveals V-Series.R-Based V-ONE Concept Prototype - dailysportscar.com
content: ShareFacebook, Twitter, Google Plus, Pinterest, Email Cadillac has revealed the V-ONE, a single-seat concept prototype based on the brand’s V-Series.R LMDh that currently competes in IMSA and the FIA WEC. Rooted in performance engineering with shared V-Series.R foundations, the V-ONE Concept, according to Cadillac, “explores how competition hardware can be translated into a driver-focused experience, while reinforcing Cadillac’s broader race-winning story across design, performance and technology.” “The Cadillac V-ONE Concept is the ultimate manifestation of a customer performance concept and is a clear sign of our ambition for the Cadillac V-Series brand in the future,” said Dominic Najafi, executive design director, Global Cadillac. The V-ONE is rooted in Cadillac’s LMDh racing programme and the V-Series.R race car. Co-developed by Cadillac Design, Cadillac Racing and chassis constructor Dallara, the concept is designed to deliver factory-level prototype performance and technology. At the heart of the V-ONE is a V8 hybrid powertrain that shares foundations with the race and title-winning Cadillac V-Series.R. It has more power than its racing counterpart, but a (lightly) simplified hybrid system which acts more as a boost to engine power and a unique aerodynamic package combining elements of different V-Series.R iterations. The concept also shares an identical chassis to the LMDh and deeper race-bred architecture in areas such as suspension, transmission and select electronics. Even with that race-derived foundation, the V-ONE is intended to be easier to operate while maintaining a similar level of performance. The aim is for its lap times to be within about 10% of the V-Series.R’s. The V-ONE’s exterior remains faithful to its race-honed sibling, while introducing refined details that make the concept feel more advanced, more technical and more tailored to Cadillac’s luxury identity. A hand-sprayed paint gradient from silver to deep navy “reflects the journey from day to night during an endurance race.” Inside, the single-seat V-ONE Concept transforms pure prototype hardware into a fully bespoke, race-bred cockpit, blending exposed carbon structure with an immersive, custom UX/UI and deeply personalized materials to create an elevated expression of Cadillac performance luxury. The steering wheel design lends to the racecar experience, complete with a button layout tailored for clients and developed by racing engineers. Other interior details include thoug material selection, including Cadillac Collection recycled fabrics, a serialized plaque on the door and a seat customized to the driver’s specifications. The Cadillac V-ONE Concept will be on display at The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering in Carmel, California on August 14, 2026. title: Arsenal v Manchester City in Community Shield and athletics gold – follow with us - theguardian.com
content: Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports Long gone are the days of an August football big bang, with all the major men’s leagues starting at 3pm on the Saturday after the Charity Shield. But in the wake of Scotland, the Carabao Cup and the National League (not forgetting assorted European qualifiers and the Super Cup), the venerable Football League itself is back – and with it Matchday live. Emillia Hawkins will look at the fallout from Friday night’s Wolves v Blackburn Championship opener (a repeat of the 1960 FA Cup final for even older nostalgia fans) and all the buildup to the rest of the programme. A Bolton v Preston derby kicks off the day’s second-tier programme, alongside League One and League Two games, though the bulk of matches kick off at the sacred hour of three o’clock. Oh, and she will also have all the latest transfer news and gossip across the men’s and women’s games. Send your thoughts to matchday.live@theguardian.com Football, and lots of it. The pick of the Championship matches is perhaps Middlesbrough v Lincoln: a side who just missed a return to the promised land hosting one that got there. Imps fans have not seen fulfilment of the spring’s “Tottenham away, olé, olé” chant but, having not played at this level since 1961, they will hardly be complaining at facing a club who were in the Premier League in 2016-17, the season that City won promotion from the National League. Scott Murray will have news from the Riverside and all the other grounds, starting with the end of the lunchtime kick-offs, with Leicester’s second ever season in the third tier starting at playoff-winning Notts County among the early League One games. It’s the penultimate night at the Alexander Stadium in Birmingham and there will be high home hopes for the men’s 100m relay at 9.33pm, after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu completed a British one-two in the individual event. A quarter of an hour later, Amy Hunt, the women’s double sprint gold medallist, will be targeting relay glory. Other British hopefuls include Amber Anning in the women’s 400m at 8.10pm and Jake Wightman in the men’s 1500m at 9.07pm. While Sean Ingle reports from the second city, Luke McLaughlin will guide you through the evening as it happens. Emillia Hawkins will be back after her Saturday morning stint to pick through that day’s events and look forward to an afternoon of action that includes the traditional Wembley curtain raiser. To the surprise of some, the Community Shield is taking place in Cardiff – not because the FA forgot to book Wembley but, it seems, because four nights of concerts from the Weeknd were more lucrative. Email matchday.live@theguardian.com with your views on whether Arsenal v Manchester City in what is now a glorified friendly carries any real significance for the new season, and anything your spies can tell us about Watford v Southampton and Burnley v West Ham. The champions take on the FA Cup winners as usual, but at the Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006, when Liverpool beat Chelsea 2-1. Twelve months ago the Reds were also taking part but went down on penalties to Crystal Palace after a 2-2 Wembley draw in which they led twice and a shootout in which Mohamed Salah disappointed with the opening kick, a set of circumstances that did, in fact, prove a harbinger of what was to come (albeit for a side who were very much still coming to terms with the death of Diogo Jota). This year Arsenal and post-Pep Manchester City lock horns, with Rob Smyth on minute-by-minute duty, while Ben Fisher and Ed Aarons report from the Welsh capital. The Championship game of the weekend is deemed by Sky to be a claret-and-blue derby, and a first English league game for Burnley’s new manager, the Belgian Nicky Hayen, a much-travelled coach in his 12th role in 13 years. In the away dugout is Nuno Espírito Santo, who couldn’t quite keep West Ham up last season. After five years of Burnley yo-yoing between the top two divisions, Hayen will have his work cut out to engender much optimism in a support base that knows too much about false dawns, while the visitors are in turmoil over events in the boardroom as well as on the pitch. Tim de Lisle is on the blog, and Will Unwin reports from Lancashire. It’s the last night of action in Birmingham and it could be a triumphant one for Britain, with a rack of relays. First up is the mixed 4x100m at 8.35pm, another chance for Britain’s individual champions to add to their earlier golds. In the men’s 4x4oom at 9.48pm, Britain has the individual champion in Matt Hudson-Smith, while Amber Anning should be the star of the women’s quartet 15 minutes earlier. Individually, Georgia Hunter Bell is in the women’s 1500m at 9.13pm, while Sweden’s pole vault showman Mondo Duplantis is in action from 7.30pm. title: The Cadillac V-One Concept Previews What a Roadgoing Le Mans Race Car Could Look Like - Car and Driver
content: If you’d like to park an LMDh prototype car in your garage, the V-One concept shows the way. Last year, when Porsche debuted the 963 RSP—a street-friendlier version of its 963 hybrid race car built for Roger Penske—Cadillac evidently took notice. Because the V-One Concept, unveiled today at The Quail,  follows the same ideological path, which is essentially, “What if we made our race car a little bit more comfortable and people could maybe drive it on the dang road?” This is, of course, an excellent proposition and a thought experiment that we fully support, even if the chances of Cadillac selling Dallara-monocoque Le Mans racers at our local dealers are probably about the same as the likelihood of reviving the Cimarron. But feel free to place your Polymarket bets now. Cadillac hasn’t explicitly said that the V-One is intended for street use, but if that weren’t the case, then why not just offer the racer as a track toy and call it a day? Ferrari already does it with the 499P Modificata, after all. Cadillac says that, compared to its V-Series.R race car, the V-One is “intended to be easier to operate while offering a similar level of performance.” We think the V-One would be significantly quicker than its race brethren, given that it’s unconstrained by pesky LMDh class rules that limit the V-Series.R to 670 total horsepower. The V-One, meanwhile, is good for 830 combined horsepower from its 5.5-liter DOHC V-8 and electric motor, and while Caddy hasn’t specified which wick got turned up, we’d suspect it was on the loud side given that LMDh cars use a standardized 67-horsepower Bosch motor-generator unit. Carryover hardware from the race car consists of most of it, including the Dallara carbon-fiber monocoque, the body, and the pushrod-actuated suspension. And, like the V-Series.R, the V-One is a single-seater, but the interior has been poshed up a bit with Cadillac Collection fabrics, a custom user interface (read: screen), and steering wheel buttons that could be tailored to a customer’s desires—you know, if there were customers. The seat would, of course, be fitted to whoever is shelling out what the V-One would cost, which we estimate would be more than a CT4. Lest you confuse your V-One with all those V-Series.Rs strewn about the Target parking lot, the concept gets unique wheels, V badging, and a sweet paint job that transitions from silver at the front end to deep navy blue at the rear to symbolize day turning to night in an endurance race. Can we figure out how to offer that on Blackwings? There is also a serialized plaque on the door. Which implies more than one V-One, doesn’t it? We hope so. Because even if nobody figures out how to put a license plate on an LMDh car, it would make for an excellent way to spice up your next HPDE run group at your local road course. And if a production V-One seems unlikely, it wasn’t so long ago that the same could be said of Cadillac building our favorite 668-hp rear-drive sport sedans. Hey, dare to dream. title: Understanding the court’s next major case on asylum seekers: Wassily v. Blanche - SCOTUSblog
content: This coming term, in Wassily v. Blanche, the Supreme Court will decide whether asylum beneficiaries are barred from obtaining lawful permanent residency if their asylum status has been terminated. Wassily is of considerable significance. While the termination of asylum status once was relatively uncommon, recent policy changes by the Trump administration have exposed far more immigrants to the risk of this. The legal dispute in Wassily, which has divided the federal courts, dates back to unclear language in the Refugee Act of 1980. The Refugee Act laid the framework for the modern asylum system and defined legal standards for asylum officers, immigration judges, and other immigration adjudicators. The act used precise, detailed language in crafting the refugee process for noncitizens outside of the United States, but Congress left internal asylum procedures more undefined, with less statutory guidance. Over time, asylum claims increased dramatically, making unclear statutory gaps more and more troublesome. Indeed, that lack of statutory clarity is front and center in Wassily. The Refugee Act specified that refugees processed outside the United States could only obtain a permanent resident green card if their refugee “admission has not been terminated.” By contrast, the act was unclear whether that same requirement also applied to asylees who had obtained asylum status from within the United States. For asylees applying to “adjust” to permanent resident status, as codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b), the Refugee Act did not mention termination at all. Instead, the act only said that the immigration official “may” grant the green card for “any alien granted asylum” who met the admissibility requirements. The act did not say whether “granted asylum” meant anyone who previously had been granted asylum or whether that phrase was limited to those with a current asylum status. Tamer Wassily left his native Egypt and entered the United States in 1993. He was granted asylum in 2000 based on his claim of persecution in Egypt as a Coptic Christian. Later, he was convicted of stalking and child endangerment, at which point the DHS sought to terminate his asylum status before an immigration judge. The immigration judge agreed and terminated this based on the finding that Wassily’s stalking conviction was a “particularly serious crime.” But the immigration judge found him eligible to adjust to a green card because the immigration statute did not contain “an explicit requirement” of current asylum status. Byron Velasquez Arreaga entered the United States in 1995 and was granted asylum. He later was convicted of multiple crimes for driving while intoxicated. The DHS sought to terminate his asylum status and scheduled an immigration court hearing. The immigration judge terminated his asylum status for particularly serious crimes. In contrast to Wassily’s immigration judge, this immigration judge found that without a current asylum status, Velasquez Arreaga could not adjust status to a green card and he was ordered removed to his native country of Guatemala. The parties appealed both cases. The Board of Immigration Appeals weighed in on the statutory confusion in a precedent decision: Matter of T-C-A-. The BIA interpreted the statute as meaning that only a noncitizen with current asylum status could adjust to permanent resident status. In Wassily’s appeal, the BIA relied on Matter of T-C-A-. It found that Wassily’s terminated asylum status made him ineligible for adjustment to a green card. The BIA also found Velasquez Arreaga ineligible for adjustment. In tandem cases for Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga, a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit agreed with the majority of circuits that only noncitizens with current asylum status were eligible for asylee adjustment. The 2nd Circuit concluded that the statutory phrase “granted asylum” was best understood to require a current asylum “status” – a legally significant term as used by Congress. The panel majority said its reading was “buttressed” by statutory context, including the Immigration Act of 1990. That act explicitly created a time-restricted exception that allowed some noncitizens to apply for green cards “regardless of whether or not such asylum has been terminated.” The circuit reasoned that this limited exception, as a “statutory note,” did not create a general rule that noncitizens could apply for permanent residency after termination. In dissent, Judge Beth Robinson adopted the minority view of the circuits on this “difficult” statutory question. She reasoned that the asylee adjustment statute meant that “any” noncitizen was eligible to adjust who previously had been granted asylum. Under Robinson’s view, the absence of the word “status” from the statutory provision must have been an intentional omission by Congress. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in June to review the statutory question of whether terminated asylees are eligible to apply for adjustment to permanent residency. In their petition for certiorari, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue that the statutory text and context are clear that any noncitizen who was “granted asylum” previously can seek permanent residence after termination. They interpret “granted” as a past tense verb, and they contend that the omission of “status” in the statutory language must be given effect because Congress knew how to include such a requirement. As broader statutory context, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga emphasize the adjacent Section 1159(c), which allows for a discretionary “waiver” of other requirements for the noncitizen’s admissibility. According to them, it would be “strange” to interpret the statute as “categorically” stripping the attorney general of that discretionary authority where the asylee’s status has been terminated. Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga also invoke the rule of lenity – the canon that a statutory ambiguity should be construed in favor of the noncitizen. They claim that lenity is especially paramount after the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright v. Raimondo, which eliminated the doctrine of Chevron deference to a federal agency’s (here, the BIA’s) reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. In an atypical move where only the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 2nd, 4th, and 5th Circuits so far have looked at this issue, Solicitor General D. John Sauer agrees that the Supreme Court should grant review. Even so, the solicitor general maintains that the 2nd Circuit was correct in interpreting asylee adjustment as limited to noncitizens with current asylum status. The government says that Congress’ intent is best understood as giving effect to the termination of asylum “status” as a bar to obtaining a green card. The solicitor general relies on the statutory note in the Immigration Act of 1990 as evidence that Congress only excepted a small subset of asylees from the general rule barring terminated asylees from adjustment of status. Without citing Loper Bright, the government disputes that the rule of lenity is applicable here at all. The solicitor general argues that the discretionary waiver at Section 1159(c) does not undermine the most natural reading of asylee adjustment because “the decision to terminate is itself discretionary” and the court should give effect to that waiver authority. The Supreme Court’s resolution of this case could impact the interests of the millions of asylum applicants with cases pending in the immigration courts and asylum offices, as well as those persons granted asylum status in recent years. Even if the Supreme Court narrowly frames this case as a discrete statutory question, it will clarify the effect of the government’s termination authority for anyone granted asylum. This is especially timely: in December 2025, the DHS announced that it would “comprehensively re-review” asylum approvals from “high-risk” countries since entry in 2021. At the end of that review, the DHS could elect to terminate asylum status. In June 2026, a federal district court vacated the DHS re-review policy, but the government is challenging that ruling. That’s not all. The case also could have broader implications for federal administrative law if the justices take an interest in the parties’ arguments about the government’s discretionary authority or Loper Bright. The Supreme Court has not yet relied on Loper Bright in deciding an immigration case. In fairness, the 2nd Circuit found no need to do so, and the Supreme Court avoided a similar issue in Urias-Orellana v. Bondi, a case that concerned the judicial standard of review for asylum “persecution” determinations. But that does not mean the court will continue to let this issue linger. Disclosure: When he was at the DOJ, the author litigated Wassily before the 2nd Circuit. He no longer has any involvement in the case or its litigation before the Supreme Court. Duncan Fulton is an Assistant Professor at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law. He has litigated more than 100 immigration cases in federal courts nationwide. title: Coach V’s Corner: I’ve Never Seen a Woodchuck - Post Independent
content: It has to be well over 30 years now that I received a call late on an August Friday night from my friend and running buddy Bob Willey. He wanted to know if I would join him the following morning for a new 5-mile race at Rifle Falls State Park called the Cheatin’ Woodchuck Chase. After immediately declining his invite, I wondered out loud if race directors would release a large group of varmints in the park, with adult human varmints in hot pursuit. Whoever catches the first one wins, or loses, depending on the temperament of that particular woodchuck. It seemed silly. After much cajoling from Willey, with a few guilt trips thrown in for good measure, I agreed to go on what was sure to be a foolhardy adventure. An adventure it turned out to be, indeed. After picking me up bright and early, Willey’s dilapidated old Audi decided to start shaking and belching smoke on Interstate 70 just west of New Castle. When the rattling and rusty old relic finally made it clear of traffic and safely to the side of the road, all I could think of to say was, “Well, at least we weren’t in an airplane!” With hopes of chasing elusive woodchucks now completely dashed, Willey and I got on U.S. 6 and 24 and jogged back to New Castle, stopping at Mattivi’s gas station. As luck would have it, a tow truck and a driver were right there on site. I had never ridden in one, but it was quite a treat hitching up the car and getting a tow back to Glenwood Springs in the big rig, with Willey giving the driver an earful about our misbegotten morning the entire way. Not to be denied, the following year, we jumped into a much more reliable vehicle and made it to the race. In the many years that have followed our abbreviated initial attempt, I have made it to more Woodchuck Chases than I can count, but I have yet to see an actual woodchuck! I’ll give it another shot this year on Saturday, Aug. 22. Sponsored once again by Rifle Recreation, the race is now a 5K and will begin and end near the Rifle State Fish Hatchery. The format is a little different this year, with runners going up the road from the hatchery for 1.55 miles and then retracing their steps back down. Start time is 9 a.m., and full details can be found at the EcoPoint Race Series on the Rifle Recreation website. Don’t forget about Saturday’s Dog Day 5K at Two Rivers Park in Glenwood Springs. The Aug. 15 run starts and finishes near the bandshell and is out and back on the Rio Grande Trail. The start time is 9 a.m., and all proceeds will benefit Colorado Animal Rescue. When I saw that Roaring Fork High School would once again field a varsity football team at the 1A level, I was reminded of all the great rivalry games between the Rams and the Glenwood Demons back when I was in high school in the late 1970s. The game between the two undefeated Northwestern League leaders in the late fall of 1978 is still the best game, with the biggest crowd I have ever witnessed at Glenwood’s stadium. It wasn’t called Stubler Memorial Field at the time because Coach Stubler was still a legend in the making as one of the assistant football coaches for the Demons. Glenwood and coach Don Miller went on to win that hard-fought game against the Rams and capture the 2A state championship a few months later on a snowy December Saturday in Glenwood Springs that was better suited for penguins than football players and fans. I wish Coach John Nielsen and the Rams the very best of luck this fall. The first game is at home in Carbondale on Friday night, Aug. 21, against Gunnison, with a 7 p.m. kickoff. I will get up to Carbondale for a few games and also catch some of the Demons this fall at what is now Stubler Memorial Field. title: Grand Theft Column V - The Daily Tar Heel
content: This week, I write that violent video games make people violent. It’s gonna be easy. Just throw together a few words scolding people who play them, maybe get a professional to back me up and you’ll be on your way to reading the kvetches before you can even say, “He phoned this one in.” Tuesday at midnight, stores released the newest in one of the most violent and popular video game series ever made, “Grand Theft Auto V.” The GameStop on Franklin Street had a swarm of college kids lined up. They’re saying it has new levels of drugs, robberies, heinous crime … and that’s just Franklin Street. (Ba dum bum.) I looked at the people in line with suspicion. With times becoming more and more violent, was I looking at future killers? I know firsthand how games can negatively impact you. I grew up playing “GoldenEye 007” in the ’90s. I spent hours playing it, becoming more and more desensitized. To this day, I still go into a karate-chopping blackout anytime I see a Russian. I spoke via telephone with James Ivory, an associate professor at Virginia Tech’s department of communication who has researched the effects of violent video games. He’d tell me what I needed to hear. “There’s very little evidence to correlate video games with serious violent crime,” Ivory said. Yes, just as I had always susp- … wait, what? Very little evidence? I could barely contain my game-playing-induced rage. After slamming down the phone and hitting it repeatedly with a bat, I decided to play the new game for myself to prove once and for all, if I spent enough time playing PS3, I could finally intimidate someone physically. In the new game, one of the main characters, Trevor, is like a meth head Tamagotchi, whom you can make do unspeakably violent things. You can even make him huff gas. The truth is … I loved it! And in real life, I’m a normal, well-adjusted gas-huffer who would never dream of acting out violently. I guess what I’m saying is, when it comes to games, we’re less like sponges, and more like … well, giant impenetrable blobs. So, if there’s very little evidence of a correlation between video games and real-life violent behavior, why does that seem like the opposite of common knowledge? I suspect most people don’t want to get to the real causes. If young people are getting more violent, video games may be a symptom, but these new parents are definitely the disease. I mean, the Greeks didn’t worry their kids would come home from “Oedipus” and gouge each other’s eyes out. They trusted them to do it because it was the honorable thing. I guess what I’m saying is, if we all band together … (nervous, sweating) … um, everything in moderation … dinners as families … (Takes out, fires gun in air) EVERYONE DOWN, THIS IS A ROBBERY!
